utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case IT-08-91-T, the Prosecutor versus Mico Stanisic and Stojan Zupljanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Good morning to everyone. May we have the appearances, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Joanna Korner, Alex Demirdjian, and Sebastiaan van Hooydonk for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Slobodan Zecevic, Slobodan Cvijetic, Eugene O'Sullivan, Simon Levett, and Denis Stoychev appearing for Stanisic Defence this morning. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Dragan Krgovic, Aleksandar Aleksic, Miroslav Cuskic, reinforced by Joyce Boekestijn and Milena Dzudovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. And if there is nothing to delay us, may we -- may we have the -- today's witness escorted into court, please. Yes, Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honours, just for the record, I have one thing. We have uploaded 1D265 translation, revised translation. Just for the record. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. So the parties -- thank you. So the -- this revised translation will now be substituted for the translation that's now a part of the record. And the parties will have been notified by e-mail yesterday afternoon that it is -- arrangements have made been to have one extended sitting today from 3.00 to 4.30. And notwithstanding the earlier expectation of the parties, we fully expect that we would be finished with this witness well before the scheduled time for adjournment at 1.45 tomorrow afternoon. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Before you take your seat, sir, would you be so kind as to read the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. You may be seated. And could you, first of all, please confirm for me that you are hearing me in a language that you understand.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can hear you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Well, I would, first of all, point out that the solemn declaration that you have just made imposes upon you an obligation to speak the truth under the pain of the penalties for perjury which this Tribunal is empowered by its Statute to impose should you give false or misleading testimony. That having been said, I, first of all, thank you for agreeing to come and testifying before the Tribunal and to assist us in our work. And I would ask you to, first of all, state your name, your place of birth, and your ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Slavko Lisica, born at Bosanska Gradiska in the village of Laminci in Bosnia-Herzegovina, that is, Republika Srpska in Bosnia-Herzegovina, on the 18th of February, 1944.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: And what is your ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm a Serb.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Have you testified previously either before this Tribunal or before any of the courts in the countries that comprise the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for His Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Sorry. Have you testified previously before either this Tribunal or before any of the courts in the countries that make up the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I haven't. I gave testimony to your investigators in Banja Luka, or, rather, they interviewed me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, we are aware of that and we have seen the transcript of that interview. Now, as would have been explained in the communications of the Tribunal officers of the Tribunal would have had with you and would have been confirmed in my former letter to you, you have been called as what we refer to as a Chamber's witness. In other words, whereas these proceedings are adversarial, that is, one side presents its evidence and then the other, there is provision for the Tribunal itself to call witnesses in order to clarify issues which may not have been clear from the testimony proffered by either side. And it is in that context that we invited you - and we are grateful, as I said, for your acceptance of the invitation - to so attend to clarify these matters. And as would have been indicated to you, the two items with which we -- on which we require your assistance are the resubordination of police forces to the army and the responsibility for an investigation and prosecution of serious crimes allegedly committed by resubordinated forces during such time of resubordination. And then secondly, your interaction with local authorities in the relevant area, including Andrija Bjelosevic and Milan Ninkovic. Now, especially since you have not testified previously, I should point out to you, and you may be generally aware of this as a matter of your own basic education and experience, that trials are -- evidence is led during a trial on a question-and-answer basis, and the necessity for this is so as to efficiently manage the presentation of relevant evidence with which the Tribunal is concerned. We are keenly aware that everyone has a story to tell. And especially persons who have not testified previously in the former setting of a court may wish to expand the answers to questions beyond what the questioner would -- is trying to find out, but I would remind you that in each case you should listen carefully to the question and only answer the question that is asked. Now, because you have been called as a witness by the Chamber, we will begin by asking you questions and, indeed, in your case, I will be asking the questions of you on behalf of the Chamber, but my brother Judges may themselves pitch in and themselves ask questions in terms of matters which I may have missed. And after I would have completed, then I would invite counsel for the Prosecution, who sits at your right, to ask their questions, such questions as they have arising out of the questions that the Chamber would have put. Following that, then the counsel for each of the two accused, and they're persons who are jointly charged in this matter, would each have their turns to ask questions of you. And at the end of it all, the Bench may have further questions arising out of what counsel would have put. In terms of time: The schedule, and again this would have been communicated to you earlier, is such that we fully expect that your testimony would be completed by midday tomorrow so that you may return to your home. The sittings for today are expected to continue until 4.30 this afternoon, which is exceptional in terms of the usual work of the Chamber. But -- and it is -- but it is not a continuous sitting. It is broken up into sessions of no longer than an hour and a half for two reasons: One is the technical necessity to change the tapes by which these proceedings are memorialised; and secondly, the breaks allow for the convenience of everyone concerned, yourself included. But notwithstanding those breaks, which are usually of 20 minutes' duration - except for the break between the first session and the last session, which would be from 1.45 until 3.00 this afternoon - the -- if at any time you yourself need to take a break for whatever reason, if you would indicate that to us, we would of course accommodate you. Now, before I go further, are there any questions that you have on which I might assist?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't have any questions. Everything you said is very clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. Would you -- perhaps you could begin by briefly telling us about your professional career. And it would be useful, as we proceed, if you would indicate to us how you prefer to be styled, whether as "Mr." or by the military rank that you last held.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I graduated from Military Academy in Belgrade and I also finished Command Staff Academy in Belgrade. That is, in -- I was trained in Yugoslavia, and I made a vow to defend the country or the state of Yugoslavia. It so happened that Yugoslavia was destroyed by NATO and it did not exist as a legal entity. The former republics of Yugoslavia became independent countries. During the war in the 1990s, I happened to be in Knin in the Republic of Croatia as chief of armoured units of the Knin Corps. That was my position. The civil war in Croatia began then, or even wider than Croatia. In Yugoslavia. As an officer of the Yugoslav People's Army, I defended the state the Yugoslavia rather than the Republic of Croatia. In Croatia there were about a million Serbs, and in Knin there was a Serbian majority. Now in Croatia there are no Serbs anymore. There are only Croats left, because the Serbs were expelled and they went to Bosnia-Herzegovina. And so on. The war continued. I defended Yugoslavia as an officer of the Yugoslav People's Army, and I held the rank of general, and I lost the war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Thank you. The --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thanks. The -- returning to the specific concerns that we have in respect of which, as I said, we expect you would be able to assist. Could you begin by telling us what your experience is of the practice in the context of the theory governing the resubordination of police forces to the military in Bosnia and Herzegovina, particularly in 1982 [sic], but even in the former Yugoslavia in general. Do you understand my question?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO LISICA
utterances.text: Yes, I understand. We are trained officers. Once you become commander of a -- any formation, and I was commander of Tactical Group 3. That's what it was called. It was a temporary formation. It was also known by the name of temporary group Doboj --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: Tactical Group Doboj.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Each formation has its area of responsibility. In that area of responsibility, the number one man is the commander, and I was commander. All units, the entire population, that is, the economic, political, and military potentials, are under the authority of the military commander of that area. All police forces were subordinated to the commander of the zone of responsibility that I had as commander of Tactical Group 3 or commander of Operative Group Doboj. The entire population, including kindergartens, schools, economic operators, everything was under the responsibility of the command of that zone of responsibility. And that included the police forces. They were also under my command. According to the Strategy of Armed Combat of Yugoslavia, where I graduated from military academy and where I completed Command Staff Academy, everything in the zone of responsibility from retired people down to children in kindergartens, medical facilities, economic operators, everything is under the command of that one man, namely the commander of the zone of responsibility. I don't know if I was clear enough. I can elaborate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Well, in terms of -- when this resubordination -- when this subordination occurred, would it be for a particular purpose, or would it be, at least in the first instance, general subordination to the commander of the zone? I have a follow-up question on that after you would have answered that part.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO LISICA
utterances.text: That's understood. How should I put it? According to the Strategy of Armed Combat of SFRY, all forces are automatically subordinated to the commander. Because we're talking about war time, not about peace. In peace, everybody goes about their own business. But since at war we all the same objectives, that is to defend the state, the -- defend the people, but this war was a civil war, and we in the Yugoslav People's Army were not trained for civil war. We were trained according to the scenario when, say, NATO were to attack Yugoslavia and how we could defend ourselves. Or if the Warsaw Pact were to attack Yugoslavia at the time. These were the kinds of scenarios that we studied. In 1968 I remember the situation in Czechoslovakia. I was second lieutenant and stationed near the Bulgarian border and we were ready to defend Yugoslavia if the Soviet Union were to attack us. I was a member of the Yugoslav People's Army then. But we never trained according to a scenario of civil war, which involves ethnic conflict, because at the time there was brotherhood and unity. That was the slogan at the time. We were all friends - Croats, Serbs, Muslims, Slovenians, Macedonians - all the peoples that lived in Yugoslavia. I was not trained to wage civil war. I applied my theoretical and practical knowledge from the Military Academy and the Command Staff Academy to act the way I would have acted towards an enemy. My former friends became my enemies, and I mean the Croats and Muslims. And I saw them as enemies. It didn't matter to me whether they were Germans, Croats, Muslims - to me, they were simply enemies who were attacking my people. And they thought that I was attacking them. And I was never able to understand that the Yugoslav People's Army became an aggressor army in their own country. Much like the US army to turn into an aggressor in California, or the German army in Styria or whichever German province. Or if the Dutch army were to attack their own country. That's what I don't understand. But that was the propaganda that was originated from the West, and those who were destroying Yugoslavia turned the Yugoslav People's Army into an aggressor in its own country. First I defended Yugoslavia. I was unable to do so. And then I started defending my own people, and that's the Serbian people. This was it in a nutshell. What I'm trying to say, that all of it was a tragedy and a misunderstanding in the Balkans. I mean, it was a civil war where you have no rule of law. Yugoslavia as a legal entity had been destroyed. Then have you no laws. You don't have a professional army. When we say "army," we didn't really have one. We had an armed people on the one hand, and an armed people on the other hand. Everybody was armed. They started fighting in kindergartens and they continued fighting all the way up to universities. It was very difficult to control that. I don't know if you understand what I'm saying. But in principle --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... if I might interrupt you to return to this matter subordination. And you may have already answered this, what I indicated was my follow-up question. When this occurred, would it have been -- when persons were subordinated to the commander of the zone, would it have been a subordination to individual military units or individually actually? Or was it once subordination occurred, then it was entirely up to the zone commander as to how to deploy these individuals?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO LISICA
utterances.text: Well, this last thing you said, talking about myself, I can say that the police forces that were subordinated to me reported to me, and I used them in combat where I had to. We are not numerous. We're not a great people. There were few of us. And the front line was long. So that every man counts. And the goals are the same - the goals of the police, the army, the educational system, politics. The goal was always to defend the people and save it from destruction by the other people. Unfortunately, that's how it went. So that police forces were directly subordinated to me. Those that were in my zone of responsibility, and I issued such orders, don't understand that -- understand this mechanically. Let's say -- let's take Bjelosevic. He's in my zone of responsibility and he comes to me and we talk like men how we can take of a -- of a situation, but my -- I have the last word in that discussion. Of course, there's no conflict there. Clearly he didn't want his police to go to the front line. But since I didn't have enough soldiers, I had to send some police officers to the front too, to at least keep certain positions in order to secure the area, to protect the population, save it from destruction, or prevent great losses. Those were talks. And it wasn't like I was the commander and I told everybody what to do. We had the same goal. We always discussed how we could solve a certain situation. But, clearly, I had the last word in my zone of responsibility. The commander is responsible in his own area of responsibility. He bears the entire responsibility for the use of the police and other institutions, such as the judiciary and, of course, including the army. But let me add so it becomes clearer to you: According to the Strategy of Armed Combat from a -- from an autonomous battalion - I don't know how much you know about military things - and up, there must be a military court. A military court takes care of all problems in the army and in the territory. Military courts. But since Yugoslavia was broken up and so was the legal system, we didn't have military courts who specialised in trying military and police forces in the zone of responsibility of any given commander. Civilian courts were not trained to try a soldier who goes AWOL, for example, or if an observer wasn't where he was supposed to be to observe and then, consequently, there are detrimental consequences; people get killed and injured. These such cases were supposed to be tried by military courts, but we didn't have any. So there was no rule of law. It was a conflict between peoples, and these people who were involved in the conflict were not trained. What you call the Army of Republika Srpska or the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina were, in fact, armed people. They were not professional armies. So we're talking about a war between one people and another. So if you have other questions, go ahead, but certainly everything in my zone of responsibility was -- was -- were things over which I had authority. Bjelosevic couldn't take decisions without consulting me, or do anything without my approval.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you for that very illuminating answer, sir. If we may take one step back. Up to this point we have been speaking about subordination in the grammatically passive sense. Could you --

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO LISICA
utterances.text: We went back.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: The -- could I ask this question: Who initiated subordination? In each case. Or did it change from case to case?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO LISICA
utterances.text: Well, I don't know how to put it. Waging a war or conducting an operation is like a live organism. You are with the same people on a daily basis, either in your office or under a tree or on the positions on some hills. You discuss your common goals. So these are requirements, the requirements of a specific moment. And at that specific moment I appeared as a responsible commander, and that applied to other commanders as well. So I would come and tell Bjelosevic, who said that the Ustasha and the Green Berets were going to attack along this and this axis. I asked him how many policemen you have. But I have to control that territory. I have this and this number of reserve police officers so let us agree amicably, and you can give me 500 policemen, I will deploy them on a certain positions, whereas, at the same time, I'm going to attack along another axis whilst you guard the already reached territory. So it's a live organism and live relationship. We were together on a daily basis, not on different planets. We belonged to the same people, we were faced with same -- the same problems. We had to reach agreements which eventually ended in me issuing an order that had to be complied with. I hope I was clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. Now, if during the time that a police unit was subordinated to your command and a resubordinated policeman committed a crime during that period of resubordination, what would be the process of, (a), reporting that crime; and, (b), the -- the investigation; and, (c), how would it -- how would it finally be dealt with?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO LISICA
utterances.text: I understood your question, though I'm not sure whether you're going to understand my answer. Since we didn't have military courts but instead we have civilian courts, in inverted commas, that was all contrary to the waging of war. When there is war, from the independent brigade, over division, up to the corps level, military courts have to be established. Had that been done, then the military courts would prosecute every crime that happened in a particular area of responsibility of each unit, i.e., a battalion, brigade, division, and corps. Military courts should have existed at all these levels. However, since the legal system of Yugoslavia was destroyed and there was no rule of law, there were attempts to deal with this on the part of the civilian courts, albeit they were not qualified to deal with the problems within the military, on the front, et cetera, especially in view of war crimes, because they didn't understand what a war crime was. So this was more in the hands of the commander to initiate, to place in custody, anyone who attempted to commit a war crime, although that was in contravention of the constitution of the former Yugoslavia. But since we were in a lawless system, it is the commander who is responsible for legal system, for prosecuting war crimes and punishing war crimes. The commander who is in command in an area of responsibility. Unfortunately, that was the situation. Had we had the proper rule of law, that would have been within the jurisdiction of military courts. I had to be the military judge and everything else. And I'm saying this not because I understood this properly, but I have to point out that we didn't have any of these institutions. Without a legal system you have nothing – the state collapses. We didn't even have a system of moral values. Some time ago, we had customary law and legal law - I don't know if it is called that exactly - but we were in a kind of vacuum of lawlessness and everything depended on individual consciousness of every commander. I'm not defending anyone, I'm just describing the situation to you. The commander is responsible for the prisoners, war crimes, and everything else in his area of responsibility, because he assumed the responsibility for that, as I did in my area of responsibility. I hope I was clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Well, you did warn me that I may have difficulty understanding your answer. In terms of what you have just attempted to explain, though, in practice, was the result that the military, or would it have been the civilian prosecutor, who would have, despite the difficulties that existed at the time and the inadequacies - that's my word not yours - of the systems in place, would it be -- was the competence in dealing with these matters that of the military or the civilian prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO LISICA
utterances.text: It would be the military prosecutor to deal with such situations. There's no place for a civilian prosecutor because he doesn't understand the issues. We had some kind of military prosecutors at the level of the corps, but that was to such a limited extent compared to the atrocities that were taking place. You need to understand that we didn't have a clash between two professional armies, but, rather, a conflict between two peoples. One mob against another. So it was very difficult for JNA officers to try and stream-line that or -- or steer it in the right direction in order to prevent losses as much as possible. Likewise, the police forces tried to make people see reason in order to avoid casualties, but it is impossible to control all the lunatics in your territory. You know this case in Norway where Mr. Breivik killed some 80 young people or so. Was that possible for the minister to control this lunatic who just went out there and killed all these kids on an island in this particular part of Europe? Likewise, we were not able to put all the lunatics under our control who put on uniforms. Some of them came from Europe and other countries simply for the purpose of looting. On the Muslim side, you had Mujahedins, Muslim Brothers, and God knows what other groups. All this was a horrible situation in the eyes of the law, and it was almost impossible for the police to prevent that. I am not trying to avoid responsibility. I did what I could, and every policeman did what they could. Now, if we're talking about reserve police, this is not a professional army either. These were armed civilians. Only 5 per cent of them were professionals. 95 per cent of them were ordinary civilians, labourers, farmers who put on uniforms. They didn't have any military training. All they had was the desire for all the birds of the feather to flock together and to defend themselves. Unfortunately, that is what happened. So can you please tell me if I was more clear this time? And I'm ready to answer any further questions you might have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. As we move on, do you recall a man by the name of Milan Ninkovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I remember all the men from my zone. Of course, yes. I forgot some of them after 20 years, but I clearly remember a Ninkovic. As I understood from some papers, it seems that we were on bad terms. He was a politician; I was a soldier. I assume that every politician, not only in the Balkans but elsewhere in Europe, tries to ingratiate himself with his own people in order to win as many votes as possible, whereas I dealt with the situation in a military way. It was a sort of conflict because basically we had different opinions. I thought that since we had a socialist system which implied social ownership, I believed that whilst the war is in progress there could be no privatisation because that would equate robbery. We have to wait for the war to end and then start building a state. You are trying here a state, Republika Srpska, which is non-existing, actually, because it hasn't been recognised. The Federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina, whereas I come from the country which is not recognised. If we start looking at all the crimes at Sijekovac and other places where the Croatian forces killed entire villagers, starting from the elderly to infants, there were no other forces and due to that we had to establish the Army of the Republika Srpska because that was the people's army, not a professional army. The JNA ceased to exist. There were some professional soldiers that happened to remain in the territory, but they didn't exceed 5 per cent. The rest, the 95 per cent, were simple people who just instinctively accepted the role of defenders of their territory. Had we had a strong and professional army, the war wouldn't have lasted for four years. That was the war of exhaustion. And once the western parties had enough of it, they started bombing the Serb army, and this is what brought the war to the end, and it was eventually followed by the Dayton Agreements. And this is what you did - in effect, you destroyed Yugoslavia. Don't think that I'm an embittered person, but I am trying to tell you that there is no intellect, no power that can control hatred. You can control people, but you cannot control hatred. Each commander had his own zone of responsibility. For example, in Srebrenica, you had international forces in control, and in spite of that, 3.000 Serbs were killed in that area. And I don't believe that anyone from Belgium or any other country who gave their contingent was tried. You simply couldn't control hatred. And that is why the Serbs were so eager to attack Srebrenica. The same applied to my area of responsibility. You can control people, but you cannot control their sentiment of hatred. And each war that happened just fueled this hate. And we hate each other now more than we did in 1990. And if another war happens, this hatred will become even worse, and I think that is going to lead to self-destruction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. You have earlier alluded to your relationship with Mr. Bjelosevic. Is there anything that you would wish to add in terms of the issues with which we are concerned today that you haven't already told us about your relationship with Mr. Bjelosevic in 1992?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO LISICA
utterances.text: We co-operated as ordinary people. One cannot speak about any friendship in that sense. We had a professional relationship. He was in charge of the internal affairs, and I was in charge of the army. We had common goals and problems, and we jointly solved them because I am that kind of person. I had the last say and each and every of my decisions had to be carried out. Bjelosevic couldn't confront me, since he had his own chain of command through the Ministry of Interior, but what does this is kind of ministry mean in a non-existent state? What does an assembly mean in a non-existent state? What does a judge mean where there are no courts? All I'm trying to say, that all the segments of society were demolished. Bjelosevic carried out my orders, but I also listened to what his requests were, and along the way we tried to find the best possible solution in order to save the people and to save the remaining political and economic institutions. So everything was based on agreement. There was no subordination relationship between the two of us. We were two men who were solving problems in a specific territory. But I did feel that I was in charge, because according to the strategy of combat, I was the responsible person because there was war. Had it been in peacetime, we would have been friends who would meet in a pub for a drink. Was I clear enough?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. That's very helpful. I don't know if the usher has yet handed to you a small folder that we have prepared for your -- to facilitate the next set of questions that I have.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO LISICA
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO LISICA
utterances.text: Everything in the interest of justice and the people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Could you look at tab 1 in that folder. And I would ask the Registrar to bring up Exhibit P1789, please. Have you -- have you seen the document at tab 1 in your folder?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO LISICA
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes. I had an opportunity to see it. Being a commander, I had an opportunity to see much more documents of this kind. This was a standard way of correspondence between the various commands and the police, and it implied joint responsibility. So please go ahead with your questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Well, if you could just expand on what you have just summarised -- on what you have just said in terms of aiding our understanding of how we should interpret this order from General Talic.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO LISICA
utterances.text: You have to read it as it says here. And it reads that the police can use only exceptionally when it is necessary to hold and strengthen the front, and that is what we did. Regardless of the order from Mr. Talic, I issued the identical orders in my zone of responsibility. The objective was not to use the police as assault units, but, rather, as units that would be holding certain lines and creating conditions for the military to take over this obligation from the police. And this is what I did, irrespective of the fact whether I had orders of the same nature from Talic or anyone else. I took my own decisions and I provided my own solutions in my area of responsibility. And I think that was a fair way of operating in a single territory, because, as I said, we had a common goal, which was to defend or people. I hope I was clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes. Well, in that vein, could you look at tab 5 in your folder. And I would ask the Registrar to bring up 1D543.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO LISICA
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: First of all, I would ask you to please confirm whether you signed this order.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO LISICA
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I did. This is my signature.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... and although you would have already - if I understood your answer in respect of the previous document - partially answered these questions, to whom was this order addressed; and how would the police have been informed of this order?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO LISICA
utterances.text: Are you referring to the formation of each detachment for the defence of Derventa town? Are you referring to that order?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... yes.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO LISICA
utterances.text: Or are you referring to General Talic's order?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: No, your order. The one that you have --

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO LISICA
utterances.text: The defence of Derventa town, supplementary order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... yes, the one that's at tab 5 in your folder.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO LISICA
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, yes, I understand. And it's been signed by me. Well, this is an order that I issued, and I think it's self-explanatory. If necessary, I can read it out for you. But this order was sent to all subordinate units and to the MUP as well, the MUP of Doboj. Or, rather, the police station. But I don't remember whether it was Derventa or any other. Anyway, all the police stations received this order, either by courier or via fax. One way or another, they received it because they would come to me to get information ... because that was a small territory. It's not as big as Australia. They were 10 or 20 or 30 kilometres apart, and we could quickly get together and exchange information. So all those concerned received these orders of mine one way or another. I used the word "gendarmerie" here because the reserve police force was not diligent enough in carrying out their duties, and I preferred to have had professional police or gendarmerie, as it is called in our people. But that's only the name. They're also made up of people and people are always the same. You know, once you liberate the territory, as it was referred to previously - but I prefer to call it when we occupied Derventa because it had been occupied by the Ustasha first - so when my units occupied this municipality, I established the post of the town commander. His duty was to restore normal operation during the interim period before professional organs took over, because there were no official authorities in this town. There was only Ustasha authority. And once you enter a town, you know that the first thing you do, you establish military authorities, whilst conditions are not created for establishing proper civilian authorities. I think you all know how it's being done, and it's the case in each and every army around the world, and our army, which was in fact an armed people, did the same.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Could you go over to your tab 6. And I ask the Registrar to bring up 1D764, which is a document dated two days later, also over your signature. And having regard to your comprehensive answer in relation to the previous document, is there anything that you would wish to add in respect of this document that's, as I said, is at your tab 6?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO LISICA
utterances.text: Not in essence. I functioned in the area which was my responsibility as commander, and that was the area of Tactical Group 3. To clarify this better: A tactical group was the equivalent to a division to western standards. Since this was in my area of responsibility, I made efforts to have the population return as soon as possible. Because in Derventa there was not a single Serb left. What -- whoever was unable to escape from the Ustasha forces was either killed or put into camps. Nobody ever made an investigation into the plight of the Serbian people in Posavina, because that's what this area is called. The Ustasha forces set up camps, and many people lost their lives there. Many families were expelled or destroyed, and they still suffer serious consequences from the traumas inflicted on them during the war. Nobody ever investigated the sufferings of the Serbian people. Probably somebody made a decision in advance that we, Serbs, are bad. And I did watch TV during the war. It was depicted that we were raping people, strangling, and so on and so forth. But when we came there, there was not a soul. I don't know who we could have raped because there wasn't anybody. First there was the Croatia army, that is, the Ustasha army. Then the Muslim forces; they were called the Green Berets. And there was the Serbian army. There were no civilians. Nothing. And what kind of propaganda this was in Europe that the Serbs are devils who rape and kill and do this and that; this was a very bad propaganda for my people and for democracy and for the truth, if you are fighting for the truth. Because if that's what you're doing, why did [as interpreted] you go there and investigate into the massacres of the people in Zadar and Zagreb and Pakracka, Dolina, and Bjelovar, where the entire staff of the JNA was killed? Colonel Kovacic was killed at his workplace. Nobody investigated into that. All the investigations went against the Serbs as the main wrong-doers. But, okay, let's leave it at that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] The -- could you look at --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thanks. I would next invite you to look at your tab 7. And, Mr. -- if the Registrar could bring up 1D765. Are you familiar with this document? Well, first of all, do you recognise it as being what it purports to be; namely, an order from General Talic?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO LISICA
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I'm familiar with it. I don't remember this specific document because each command got a written document daily. I believe that there was some two tonnes of documents in all. This was found in my bag. That's where it happened to be. And the entire documentation is with the corps. From my command, since there was daily reporting, so on 360 days, there were 360 reports. And 360 times four years, you can imagine how that adds up. There was a report to the corps commander and a report to General Mladic. I knew him personally from Knin. We know each other as people and as officers. He demanded that I send an identical copy as the one that I was sending to the corps to him also. I don't know where he was. In Han Pijesak, I think, his command post was. So there is about a thousand documents. And your investigators weren't able to find it. Actually, they didn't feel like going through the heaps of documents, and this one happened to stay behind in my bag, and I gave it to them. But they should have dug deeper in the documentation of the corps, and they would have found a couple of thousand signed by Colonel Lisica. That's me. There must be 5.000 documents at the corps command. And then you would be clear about who did what to whom during that unfortunate war. However, arbitrary stories, second-hand, you know, but this document doesn't mean anything to me. I drafted such documents as the responsible person to my subordinate units and the police units in my responsibility. And that includes Bjelosevic. And we had a good relationship; only, I had the last word. That's how it was during the war. And no one of my subordinates can be held responsible. Only me, because I issued the orders. If a corporal commits a criminal offence, he can't be held responsibility without me being held responsible, because it's my responsibility. And that's how people knew me in my area of responsibility. I don't shirk my responsibility. I only acted in accordance with human laws and God's laws, and, of course, military regulations, and those were the regulations of the Yugoslav People's Army, where I was trained too. I wasn't trained in the American army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. I would next invite you to look at tabs 2, 3, and 4. And I'm not sure, having regard to the technical limitations of us only being able electronically to bring up one document at a time, but it would be 1D263, 1D264, and 1D265. And my question would relate to all of those documents. So perhaps the Registry should bring them up sequentially.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO LISICA
utterances.text: Yes, I see. It's okay. Withdrawal of the police from combat operations. Bjelosevic requested that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... if you would just --

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO LISICA
utterances.text: Many of my commanders --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... if would you just give me a moment, sir, while the electronic version is being loaded, and then I will phrase my question.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO LISICA
utterances.text: Sure, go ahead. I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: If we could deal with them -- with your reading of the documents one at a time. When you are through with tab -- your tab 2, which is Exhibit 263 for our purposes, if would you please let me know. And then I'd ask the Registrar to move on to the next document, and so on.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO LISICA
utterances.text: I've read it. I'm familiar with the contents of this request. It's about withdrawal of the police from combat. You can ask your question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes. Could we then move on to the next document, which is Exhibit 264. Your tab 3.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO LISICA
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: And when you --

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO LISICA
utterances.text: Yes, I know this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: And then Exhibit 1D265, which is your -- sorry, 1D265, which is your tab 4.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO LISICA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: So what we have here, and correct me if I'm wrong, is an exchange between yourself and Mr. Bjelosevic. And the --

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO LISICA
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: My first question is whether you were still -- whether you were still commander of Tactical Group 3 at this time?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO LISICA
utterances.text: I was. I was commander of Tactical Group 3. Well, let me tell you like a man. This is a small part of the puzzle. When you put it on paper, then you get the impression that it carries more weight because it stays behind in archives and then later you can be held responsible. We had such meetings daily. And this is just a very small part of my dealings with Bjelosevic and the commanders of the civilian or military police, the commanders of brigades and battalions in my zone of responsibility. He requested officially, not merely orally, because later on nobody will admit to it. Probably his subordinates exerted pressure on him because they wanted to get out of combat. Let's take military units from Bosanska Gradiska. The president of the municipality and the presidents of the parties came to me daily asking me to let their people go so they wouldn't have to fight anymore. In a civil war, fear is incredibly great. Everybody is afraid of war and afraid of death, and everybody wants to stay as far as away from the front as possible. Some of them fled, and we didn't have military courts to sanction them. Some of them fled to Belgrade, others to Vienna. Some maybe came here and may still be here, actually. Only to flee from the war. And now we are being held responsible for crimes that we committed. But tell me where and who committed them. But we were unable to control the armed people and we were unable to control their hatred. We could not control the criminals. We tried to, but we couldn't. Just like you, here, weren't able to control that guy who killed 80 people on that beach. And, yeah -- and we had such people armed in great numbers. But let me tell you something else. According to the Strategy of Armed Combat of Yugoslavia, where I was trained, if I were to order soldiers to enter this room and kill you all, just for -- to give an example, they were not obliged to carry out my order, because if they did, they would commit a crime. And they could be held responsible for executing that order. So everybody has the right to refuse an order, the consequence of which would be a crime. You cannot order anybody to execute prisoners of war. Of course, I can go crazy and issue such an order, but the one who is supposed to execute them must know that he has the right to refuse such an order. I'm talking about professional soldiers, of course. But these reserve forces, the armed people, they know no laws and regulations. This applies to Muslim forces, Serbian forces, or Croatian forces. I had some prisoners, members of Croatian forces, and they told me the very same thing as the Serbs who were taken prisoner and then exchanged. If you are taken prisoner by an active duty officer or an NCO, Serb, Croat, or Muslim, doesn't matter, then you stand a chance of surviving. But if you get caught by a reservist - we call them reservists because whoever was, I don't know, a waiter in civilian life and now has the rank of captain - if you are taken prisoner by such a one, you don't stand a chance. You'll get killed. If you are taken prisoner by an active-duty police officer, it's all right, but if it's a reserve police officer, you don't stand a chance. That's how it was. But if you think it was otherwise, then prove it to me. Go ahead. I'm talking -- I'm saying to you what was happening on the ground. And I'm sorry it was that way. And all my energy, not just mine, but that of the active-duty police, professional police, and all the professional soldiers, officers, and NCOs, they were more worried about preventing crimes than executing some combat assignment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: General, can I just follow up on what you have just told us. In the letter which you have in front of you signed by Mr. Bjelosevic, it appears that what he is saying is that it was because his policemen had been assigned to your front line that there was now extensive looting and disorder in Doboj. Do you agree in his assessment here? In other words, if the policemen had not been reassigned to the front line but would have stayed home in Doboj, would the looting and disorder not have taken place?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO LISICA
utterances.text: Well, I can agree with his assessment, that probably there would be less of that. Especially if we're talking about active-duty police officers. But if only reserve police officers stayed back in Doboj, then he was unable to do anything with him. And that was the same with reserve police -- military police. I was able to impose law and order only with active-duty military police. But it's important for all of us to know that once a state falls apart and there are no more laws, then everybody takes the law into their own hands. And then we're talking about pillage, plunder, and no more than that. There is no responsibility. I went into a village and asked the people, But why are you plundering? And they would answer, But what are you talking about? There's no state any more. But there's me, I said. And who are you? I'm a JNA officer. And they would reply, But there's no more JNA. And I don't wish anyone to go through the same that my people went through. Educated people in Europe cannot understand the calvary we went through when we lost our state and the rule of law. I'm a man who honours the law, and I would like to die in this country when there is the rule of law. I live in Bosnia-Herzegovina now, but there is no rule of law there. Some perpetrators of atrocious crimes during the war are not standing trials in Bosnia-Herzegovina. There's your judge over there, I mean, an international judge, who says that a column of the JNA, that is, I'm -- we're talking about youths of 19 years of age, are a legitimate target for thugs to be killed by them. And so this column --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... General --

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO LISICA
utterances.text: -- was a legal target for the Green Berets. Not even now we have a legal system. 20 years after the war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: General, please keep your answers short. The reason I'm asking this to you is that there seems to be a slight contradiction in what you are saying. Namely, on the one hand you're saying that there were a lot of thugs who were looting and acting on their own and you couldn't control them. On the other hand, you're saying that, well, these people could be - at least to some extent - controlled if there had been sufficient police forces to secure law and order. So my question is, to you, to give us a picture of what the situation really was. Are you saying that looting and disorder took place everywhere and that, really, nobody could prevent that, not even if there was police available? Or are you saying that looting and disorder could, in fact, be controlled and prevented, to some extent, if only there had been enough qualified manpower in the police forces available in the area? Now, which is it?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO LISICA
utterances.text: If we had had enough professional police, and I'm talking about the professionals from peacetime, then we would have been able to prevent looting. Professional police means not reserve police. Not armed people. Then it would have been possible to prevent looting to a great extent. Where there were professional officers and NCOs, looting was prevented. But there's no contradiction here. I'm saying that the situation was favourable for disorder and injustice, because the institutions had been destroyed. They couldn't function because the state was no longer there. During the war, we were trying to set up a state, and that's the Republika Srpska, which it, as yet, unrecognised. It's an entity within Bosnia-Herzegovina. Based on the experience of the former Yugoslavia, we tried to set up a system. But the setting up of a legal system is slow. And even today Bosnia-Herzegovina is an internationally recognised country - although it had never been a country before - it is not a state with a rule of law. And if you have international judges, that's one thing. But nobody does anything with regard to the law. Even nowadays there's looting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you, General.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: We've reached the point where we must take our first break. We will rise, and return in 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Before I invite counsel for the Prosecution to cross-examine, I don't know if either of my brother Judges have any further questions of the witness. Yes. Yes, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: General, you were interviewed by the Office of the Prosecutor almost exactly a year ago. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO LISICA
utterances.text: More or less, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And when you arrived here, you were given a copy of that interview which had been typed up in your own language. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO LISICA
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And you were then spoken to by one of the legal officers in this case, Mr. Cengic, who asked you if you'd had an opportunity to read that interview; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO LISICA
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And you told him that you had read it.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO LISICA
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And you were asked if there was anything that you wanted to add or alter, and you said no. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO LISICA
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So you stand by the answers you gave to the Office of the Prosecutor in Banja Luka last year.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO LISICA
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you. Can I just ask you this: You live in Banja Luka and have done for many years; do you know a gentleman called Mirko Bojinovic, who used be with the -- the SNB in 1992?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO LISICA
utterances.text: No. Maybe we know each other, but his name is not so much in my memory as the names of Bjelosevic and others. I cannot remember if I really do know him or not.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO LISICA
utterances.text: Probably he knows me.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I want to know whether between February of last year and coming here earlier this week you've had any conversation with him. Mr. Bojinovic, this is. I'll come on to Mr. Bjelosevic in a minute.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO LISICA
utterances.text: No. I didn't have any conversation. I don't know what we would have talked about anyway. Nobody asked me to do that. I felt no need to that because I'm not that kind of person. I always speak my mind, and what I said in Banja Luka and what I'm going to tell you here today, I believe that I spoke the truth. Maybe I omitted some of the things due to the lack of time, what I wished to say, but I stand by what I did say.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Mr. Bjelosevic; have you seen or spoken to him between February of last year and coming here this week?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO LISICA
utterances.text: I think we talked once. But he lives in Doboj, and whenever he comes to Banja Luka, he rings me up and we have coffee together as friends. We discuss family issues. Sometimes we tackle the issue of The Hague because he had been to The Hague, but I wasn't very much interested in hearing that. And I'm telling you the truth. So since this interview with this investigator and now, we did meet once. I think it was three or four months ago. But the truth is that whenever he comes to Banja Luka, he contacts me and we discuss ordinary things. I asked him about the situation in Doboj, economically, and in other aspects.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did you -- you told us that sometimes you tackle the issue of The Hague. Did he tell you about his experience of giving evidence at this court?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO LISICA
utterances.text: No, he didn't speak about it. Although he did try to talk about this to me, but I refused because, in my view, The Hague Tribunal is biased. It is trying only the Serbs and not members of other peoples from the Balkans. This is my opinion. Whether it is an objective one or a subjective one, we can debate that. But I don't think that -- rather than achieving reconciliation among the peoples of the Balkans, it has worsened the situation. Because when you watch TV sometimes -- all right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... I'm sorry, General, but we need to stick to --

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO LISICA
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... we need to stick to the topics. Right. Now, the last question on this: Since you were informed by the Trial Chamber that you were being asked to come to court to testify, have you had any discussion with Mr. Bjelosevic about the nature of your evidence?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO LISICA
utterances.text: No. I think that last I saw him was three, four, or five months ago, but, as I told you, this is a common practice whenever he comes to Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... no, I didn't -- yeah. I -- no, stop. I didn't ask whether you'd seen him. I asked you whether you had had any discussion with him, and that includes the telephone.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO LISICA
utterances.text: No, no. We did not discuss it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Can we then very briefly just flesh out your career for a moment, about which you were asked about earlier this morning. Between 1988 and 1992 you were chief of the Armoured Mechanised Unit in Knin; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO LISICA
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You then transferred in 1992 to what was still, before the declaration of the VRS, the 5th Krajina Corps, was it not? The Banja Luka Corps.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO LISICA
utterances.text: Yes, yes. After the Kupres operation. I was conducting Kupres operation, and after that I was transferred to the Banja Luka Corps.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. And for a short period of time, is that right, you were at the Manjaca training ground, as it then was, helping to train or set up the 2nd Armoured Brigade?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO LISICA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And then, as you told the Court, you were appointed as the commander of Tactical Group 3 in the Doboj area. And that was in June, was it not, of 1992?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO LISICA
utterances.text: Yes. On the 24th of June.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And you remained there until you replaced Colonel Simic, as he then was, as commander of the operations group in Doboj; and that was in 1993.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO LISICA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Now, is this right: The size of Tactical Group 3 was somewhere between 10- and 15.000 troops?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO LISICA
utterances.text: That's right. Depends on how many of them are present. You always have a third of them absent for various reasons. Because, as I said, those were ordinary people bearing arms, as they had to leave to tend to their cattle, or toil the land, or whatever. Because they were not professional army.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... all right. And just, again, roughly, could you tell us, how large was Operation Group Doboj? Roughly.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO LISICA
utterances.text: Roughly speaking, around 30.000.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So all together in that area there were not less than 40.000 armed military persons in -- in that area, during 1992?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO LISICA
utterances.text: Well, it's very difficult to say precisely, but I think this is an approximate number. And if you add active and reserve police officers, the total number of uniformed personnel was around 40.000. When I say "uniformed," I mean those who were not professionals but were issued uniforms. As I said, an armed people.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I just want to ask you to look, please, at one document in relation to your transfer into the Banja Luka Corps.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Could we please have up on the screen 65 ter 20409. And it's document number 4 in the Prosecution bundle.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: This document is from the 1st Krajina Corps, as it become, dated the 11th of June, to the Main Staff, and it's giving a list of those who have transferred from the JNA into the VRS in that corps. Could we look, please, at, in English, page 7 -- sorry. Page 8, I beg your pardon. And in the -- I think it's the same in B/C/S. No, it's page -- it says page 15 at the top, and I think that's probably right. Yes. Thank you very much. And is that your name that we can see there, if you look at the left-hand side, at number 8?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO LISICA
utterances.text: Number 8, Lisica. Yes, yes. Colonel, OMJ, SSNO.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now can we please go back, please, to the first page.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO LISICA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The officers that we see there, beginning with Talic, then a Lieutenant Ratko Jovic, Bosko Kelecevic, Dragan Marcetic, Gajic, Babic, and so on, did you know these officers?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO LISICA
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Are these all experienced officers, some of whom had been certainly with you in Knin or in Western Slavonia, during the Croatian conflict?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO LISICA
utterances.text: When the Croats attacked the Yugoslav People's Army? Is that what you mean?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, I'll -- for the moment, I'll let you say that. Exactly. When you say the Croats attacked the JNA. Were these officers all officers who had experience of the -- of the conflict in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO LISICA
utterances.text: Well, I'm not as sure about all of them, all these names that I'm looking at. I think that Talic was in Stara Gradiska. Jovicic [as interpreted], I don't know. Kelecevic was serving in Zagreb, and he barely managed to escape. Marcetic was at the training centre, and so on and so forth. But if you're referring to any war experience, I don't think that none of us had any. And I'm referring to experience in a civil war, because we were trained differently.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I quite understand -- I -- I understand entirely that the training of the JNA --

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO LISICA
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Just pause, please, sir. I understand entirely that the training of the JNA envisioned an outside enemy and not a, what you call, a civil war. All I'm asking is: Were these officers whom you knew experienced JNA officers?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO LISICA
utterances.text: Generally speaking, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, if we look, please, at the next page. Did you know Colonel Vukelic?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO LISICA
utterances.text: Yes. The late Colonel.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. What about Lieutenant-Colonels Radman and Jakupovic?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO LISICA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: What about Colonel Stevilovic, at number 42?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO LISICA
utterances.text: I never made his acquaintance, but I heard at the beginning of the war that he was killed.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Were these -- those who you did know, and it's a long list, were you -- would you describe these as trained and experienced officers?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO LISICA
utterances.text: Yes, I would say that they were trained and experienced officers.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, may this document please be admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, one question only. In principle, given the contents of this document, I have no objection. I would just like to make one remark. We received this document from the OTP recently. And according to Rule 68, it should have been disclosed to us earlier in order to address it with Colonel Kovacevic, because it expressly deals with the number of officers.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, this was -- it was on the list for one of the earlier witnesses, and I can't remember which, so it has been disclosed sometime before. But as there's no objection, Your Honours, may this be admitted and marked, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Exhibit P2455, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. Now, before you went to Doboj as head of Tactical Group 3, did you attend a meeting in early June to do with Operation Corridor?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO LISICA
utterances.text: I think I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And was this the first occasion that you met Mr. Bjelosevic?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO LISICA
utterances.text: I don't remember meeting him at that particular occasion. I didn't know the man. We may have met following my arrival from Knin, or, rather, from Banja Luka to Doboj, but this was a large meeting in which as many as 100 people may have participated. But since we were neither interested in each other, I don't think that we met until the time when I became commander of TG 3, and that is when he came and we met.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. Well, I remind you of what you said in interview about this. This is page 81 in English and page 70 in the B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry, I forgot to give the number. I was waiting for it to come up. Please, could we have up, please, 65 ter 30012.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Could we have a tab number, please?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Tab 1.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And I think that it's in the Defence's as well, normally.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. You'll see there the question, after Mr. Bjelosevic, you were explaining, Mr. Bjelosevic had more dealings with the corps.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO LISICA
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yep. When did you actually first meet him? So you then say: "So he came to meet me. "Q. How long after you arrived in Foca would that -- would that have been?" And you said: "Two to five days. I think he was also present or it might have been the occasion that we first met where we sat down to decide how will we go about to pierce of corridor. If you recall, when we had the meeting at the agricultural co-operative, I'm assuming, because Martic was also there from the Republika Srpska Krajina, so I'm assuming that the Doboj head of CSB must have been there. "Q. This also involved to a certain extent the Banja Luka CSB. Would Stojan Zupljanin have been at this meeting?" Your answer, over the page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KORNER
utterances.text: I think it's in -- in B/C/S ...

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: It's the same page in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Oh, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: "It's possible, but I'm not certain ..." "Q. But you think Bjelosevic was also there?" And you say: "I think he was. He was not taking notes ... there were a multitude of people ..." Now, is that right?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO LISICA
utterances.text: Yes, that's what it says. I really wasn't interested to know who was present there. There were my school friends there, people with whom I attended academy. We got together and chatted. But I didn't know any of those people. He was probably there, given that he held the post that he did.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, because this meeting was actually held, wasn't it, in Doboj? As you put it, these were the hosts. Doboj was the host.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO LISICA
utterances.text: Yes. The president of Doboj municipality. That how it works [as interpreted].

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And was somebody called Mr. Ljubicic there as well?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO LISICA
utterances.text: Well, Ljubicic was the municipality president, and he had the rank of a reserve major.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And what about Nikola Perisic, president of the Teslic municipality?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO LISICA
utterances.text: I met him later. He may have been there as well. And all these people that were there were invited by the corps commander. I only exchanged greetings with the people I knew from my past, from my school days. But as for the others, I can't tell you either way whether they were there or not. I don't see the point.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Okay. Let's sum this up. This was a meeting of the military, the political, and the police to plan Operation Corridor, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO LISICA
utterances.text: Well, that was more in a theoretical sense. I didn't even know what my role was going to be. A decision was made at that meeting to resolve the problem. Since the corridor was cut off, the corridor leading to Belgrade and Bijeljina --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... yes --

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO LISICA
utterances.text: -- the instruction came from the Main Staff. But I explained all this to you, and I think it's clear to everybody present here. So a decision was taken on how to free these communications to gain uninterrupted access to Bijeljina and further on towards Belgrade and Serbia, because we belonged to the same people and we were fighting for the state of Yugoslavia at the time. Both the politicians and myself.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: General, can I just remind you, as the Judges reminded you: Please keep your answers short and just answer the question. The answer to my question is: This was a meeting to plan or to make arrangements for Operation Corridor. Wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO LISICA
utterances.text: You're right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, I want to deal with something that, as we will see, caused you some aggravation. During the whole of 1992 and indeed 1993 there was never a declaration, was there, of a state of war in the Serbian republic [sic]?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO LISICA
utterances.text: The Republika Srpska was not a state.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I said in the -- I don't know how it was translated, but I said in the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. A state of war was not declared, was it? Simply an imminent threat.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO LISICA
utterances.text: Well, what I'm saying is that since the Republika Srpska, even today, is not recognised as a state, I don't know how it could have declared the state of war. We probably should have declared the state of war in what we were calling the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Why this wasn't done is a question to put to the supreme commander, Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No. But, sir, it was something that concerned you a great deal, wasn't it? because it limited your powers, the powers that you have so graphically described to the Judges this morning.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO LISICA
utterances.text: Well, clearly, once the state of war is declared, or the state of imminent threat of war, and so on, then there's a legal basis for you to use all the resources of a given territory for armed combat. In other words, for war. The way it was, you had no legal basis to use what you think you should use. So I insisted that the state of war be declared, although we were not a state. In the municipalities where I was, I told every president of those municipalities that I consider the actual situation to be the state of war and that, to my mind, we were at war. Of course, that was not official. But the municipalities where I really was, they were -- in reality they were at war.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yeah. All right. But the fact remains, and this is -- you mention this on a number of occasions in the interview, and I'll remind you of one of them, that no state of war had been declared. So what you described to the Judges as every -- everything from the kindergarten -- down to the kindergarten being under your command was not in fact the case, if it ever was, but certainly not in the 1992, was it? Much -- well, perhaps can you answer that question.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO LISICA
utterances.text: It was as if there had been a state of war, in practice. Theoretically, or legally speaking, it was not that way because it wasn't declared. But in practice, to my mind there was a state of war because everybody had to carry out my orders, without any contradiction.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, well that's what you would have liked, but it's not actually what happened, was it?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO LISICA
utterances.text: It was like that. I'm sorry, were you there? You would have done what I told you too.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, well, I'm going to come on to your personal characteristics in a moment, General. But, you see, what you said at one point, when you were asked this - and this is at page 49 of the interview in English and page 41 in B/C/S - you were asked -- you talk about the war. "You were aware, were you, there was no state of war that had been formally declared." And your rely was: "I am aware of that, which was very strange on the part of the leadership, both military and civilian. I was one of those who insisted that it be declared. I had no support, which is why I had to retire, not only because of that." Is that right?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO LISICA
utterances.text: Yes. So what? What about it? That's exactly how it was.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. Now, let's have a look at another time you made -- this is December of 1992. Could you have a look, please, at part of Mladic's notebook, which is, please, P1764. At tab 35. And this is him recording for the 5th of December. So what page is that in ... it's page 228. Now, this is a briefing -- oh, wait a minute, we'll just wait -- yeah, it's coming up. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO LISICA
utterances.text: Can you -- yes, in Serbian, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It's coming up in Serbian. But slowly. Well, there should be a --

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO LISICA
utterances.text: Oh, I can't read this handwriting.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... all right. Well, there should be a typed copy.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO LISICA
utterances.text: Well, if you can show me that one. Yeah, I can see it says Lisica.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Are you family with General Mladic's writing?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO LISICA
utterances.text: Yes. But I was never able to read it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO LISICA
utterances.text: I had a courier and always asked to him, Do read out to me what Mladic says. Because I write in Latin script and he uses Cyrillic script.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Do you recognise his writing, though?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO LISICA
utterances.text: I think it is his hand.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Well, I'll read you what we've got and then we'll try -- there is a typed copy in your language, but ... It's you speaking on the 5th of December. And you say: "The military and political authorities in Teslic have united. "A state of war should be proclaimed and order should be established behind the front." Do you remember saying that? Do you remember this meeting where you had a go at just about everybody?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO LISICA
utterances.text: I was saying that every day, day in, day out. That's nothing new. That was my position.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yep. And you had a go, if you understand that, if it can be translated, against somebody called Mr. Popovic, Mico Stanisic, Goran Bubic, and General Talic, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO LISICA
utterances.text: Where do you read that from?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Do you see --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Perhaps we can give, in all fairness to the witness, the -- [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yeah. Yes, the typed copy. Well, actually not -- [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, not the typed copy, or maybe this copy -- [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I've got a typed copy in.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Where am I having a go at these people?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Do you see, your name is underlined and this is you speaking, isn't it? General Mladic is making a note of what you say.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO LISICA
utterances.text: I don't know this Mico Stanisic. I didn't know him then. I couldn't speak about a man whom I didn't know. I don't know him even today. Is he about? I knew Bjelosevic, Goran Bubic. I don't remember that one. He may have been president of the SDS. But general -- I spoke generally that I disagreed with the SDS policy, if I said that. But I probably did. But these are not my words. Maybe that’s what he thought, maybe I spoke and since he knew those names, he wrote down the names, whereas I was speaking generally that the SDS at Teslic did this or didn't do that or whatever. Whereas I never knew this Mr. Stanisic.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, you say that. But one of your obsessions, wasn't it, during this period --

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO LISICA
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Just a moment. Just a moment.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO LISICA
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. What do you want to say about Bubic? Very quickly.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO LISICA
