utterances.text: I don't remember Bubic. I don't know him. Goran Bubic. I may have met him casually, but ... I did know Talic. I knew Jovo Popovic. He was a self-styled lieutenant-colonel.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... all right.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO LISICA
utterances.text: I don't know all of these people.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... but your obsession, or one of your obsessions during this period, 1992, was what you considered to be the -- the looting that was taking place for personal gain without anybody doing anything about it. That was your -- your -- one of your obsessions, wasn't it? Or one of your -- leave out the word "obsessions." One of your great criticisms.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO LISICA
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... and what you're --

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO LISICA
utterances.text: You know something? I can clarify, if you let me.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... no. Well, clarify what?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO LISICA
utterances.text: Explain why I had held this opinion. During the war, a self-proclaimed government - and that's what it was to me - you don't have a state and you have an assembly. And then the assembly adopts a law that there should be privatisation during the war. Those were state-owned enterprises that were supposed to turn private. To my mind, that was theft. During the war, there can be no transfer of property, and I considered that theft generally. Whoever was in power, when I was angry, I called these people thieves. That they were stealing. Whoever implements privatisation during the war is stealing. And you're right if you call it an obsession. Because once the war ends, then we can go about normal things. But during the war, that's nonsense. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. I want to return, however, to the question. As I say, on a number of occasions during the interview you talked about this. The difference between an imminent threat of war and a state of war. You did not --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mrs. -- Mrs. Korner, before you move to that point, I would like to ask the witness -- Does the witness have a -- a printed copy now in Serbian?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: He has both, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay. Could the witness read the last part that starts with: "Talic." The last entry on -- on this -- this page in English.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I read it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Can you read it aloud so that it can be translated, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Okay. It is said about Lisica that he is the greatest profiteer. These are Talic's words. That he looted Derventa Brod, that he stole the cattle and drove it to Levita, that he stole the monuments and sold either it or some other things to -- to farmers. But this is a total lie. If you want me to explain?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... no, no, thanks, General. It's -- it's just because -- because I wanted to check something. Mrs. Korner, did I understand you well that it is your position that all these entries are the General's ideas or words?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. All of the -- it's rather oddly phrased in English, but it is actually -- our understanding is it's Colonel Lisica talking about all these people, and General Mladic making a note. And this is also -- this is Colonel Lisica, as he was then, saying Talic is saying about me, he's talking about himself in the third person.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Look at -- look at the reading by the witness just a moment ago is exactly the opposite.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, I don't think it is. I hope this is not coming off my time --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: And that's how I read the English as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No. I -- Your Honour, I hope this is not coming off my time. But, anyhow ...

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Colonel, this is you, isn't it, complaining that Talic has said these things about you?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO LISICA
utterances.text: I can only say that Talic was an SDS member, to my knowledge, and that we had political differences, because I didn't belong to any one party. I had been a member of the League of Communists of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Don't worry about that, Colonel. But it's because of the phrasing in this notebook. It's -- General Talic wasn't speaking there, was he? It was you complaining that Talic was defaming you.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO LISICA
utterances.text: Yes. My authority was great. Well, relatively, given the circumstances. And then probably - but you should ask him to make sure - he was afraid of my authority and my prestige and he blackmouthed me and said that I was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... please, General, General --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- doing dishonourable things.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... General, please, it's just about -- well, it's so that we can get clear about what is said here. So you answered by the affirmative. You said, Yes, this is me complaining about Talic telling lies about me. Is that right? That's the only thing we need to know here. Is this note about you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is probably correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Correct, correct, correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, [indiscernible] -- I will do it because I asked the same question when I looked at the entry, so I got somebody who is a B/C/S speaker to tell me. Now, can we go back to the state of war and imminent threat of war. Your only reason for complaining right up until December 1992 and onwards that no state of war had been declared was because you didn't leave -- you weren't legally able to exercise the powers that you described to the Court because there was no state of war, that is, control of everything and everybody. That's the reason for it, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO LISICA
utterances.text: In practice, I had control over everything and everybody. But I didn't have a legal basis.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. Now, this is what I'm coming to. Because of your personality, General, which, as you yourself said, you were a strict officer and a good commander, you ran or tried to run your area as though there had been a state of war declared. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO LISICA
utterances.text: Yes, that is exactly right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. But unfortunately it didn't quite work like that, and I'm going to come on in a moment to the question -- the whole question you were asked this morning about resubordination. But I want to start with some other matter. You told the Court this morning that during 1992 the military courts weren't operating. Now, were you aware that the military court in Banja Luka was operating from the 19th of July of 1992?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO LISICA
utterances.text: I knew that there was a military court in Banja Luka with a very small capacity. According to the rules of armed combat - I explained that to you - from an independent battalion up, there should be a military court. Since I'm a military person and use military language, I don't know if these judges are able to understand the state of war, or, rather, the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina. If these judges are civilian judges, they probably understand it at a theoretical level but not the practical duties of a soldier, an officer, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Don't worry about that. All, at the moment, that I'm asking you is whether you were aware that there was a military court operating on the 19th of July, and you said yes. Were you familiar at all with any of the criteria for military prosecutors that had been issued? Had you ever -- did you ever see them?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO LISICA
utterances.text: No, I have never seen them.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. And it -- would it would be right to say - and this is not a criticism at all, General - that you don't actually have anything to do with the operation of military courts?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO LISICA
utterances.text: Nothing whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Now, you were asked this morning about the question of town commands. You were shown two documents about it, in Derventa. Can I just read you what you said in interview and see if that is, as you told us, still your position about the question of town commands.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: This is at page 35 in English and 30 in B/C/S. Sorry, 30012, please; 65 ter.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, you were asked about -- in fact, the original question was about joint operations where the police were not resubordinated to the military. And you said: [As read] "in principle, if we are talking about a populated area, you would appoint a commander, like I appointed one in Derventa. Which in no way affects the tasks the civilian police is supposed to conduct to preserve peace and order, just as I appointed the town commander for Brod. The police would conduct their own affairs of prevention of robberies, murder, et cetera, but regardless of that, you would appoint a town commander, and the town commander is supposed to co-ordinate the tasks and supposed to work together. The police is supposed to maintain public law and order while the town commander specifically is supposed to co-ordinate and organise, first of all, battle-field clean-up, general removal of effects of combat operations upon the town itself. And then, if possible, he is supposed to also organise the work of utilities, et cetera. "Q. So, in fact, a town commander would take over the civilian part of the municipality until this is installed again? "A. 100 percent correct. Until everybody who is supposed to do their own jobs returns and starts doing them." And then further down the page, you were asked: "A town command is completely separate from a garrison command. "Correct. A town command is a temporary body that exists until civilian life returns to normal." Those are the answers you gave last year. Do you still stand by them?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO LISICA
utterances.text: Yes, I do stand by them fully.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... thank you.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO LISICA
utterances.text: I agree with myself.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. Can we then look, please, at one short matter about, as it were, police/military co-operation. The question of prisoners. And this is the next page, please, in English, and in B/C/S also. At the bottom of the page in English you were asked: If you took prisoners, what would you do with them? And then you said: "According to all military regulations, we're talking about a group of enemy combatants, soldiers that you captured, a report has to be made to the commander."

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: We need to go to the next page in English, please. But it's still the same page in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: "The commander orders prisoners to be removed to the rear post -- rear command post. From the rear command post, they would be taken to ... free territory, the free territory that we consider to be Serb free territory, and turned over to the civilian authorities. From that [sic] moment on, they would be in charge of the civilian legal bodies." And then further down the page, you were asked: "You are talking about what sort of prisoners? Those who were in uniform on those who were apparently not in uniform in civilian clothes?" And your answer: "The soldiers that would have been captured during combat operations would still be turned over to the civilian prisons. That's how it functioned in my area of operations. I can only be responsible, and I can only talk about what passed, transpired in my zone of responsibility." And then you explain how you didn't have the resources to feed the prisoners. You were later asked --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Perhaps we ought to go to the next page in English and also in B/C/S, please, to page 32.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You said -- you were asked about the -- you were mentioning the Geneva Convention. And you said that: [As read] "prisoners should be turned over to certain authorities that exist in the liberated or free territory. Because in the area of responsibility ... you only have military authorities. Everything outside an area of responsibility is controlled by the civilian authorities, and my zone of responsibility -- my area of responsibility was so small that I wouldn't have had the needs to detail with a small number of captured military of the enemy ..." And then you were asked --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Next page, please, in English.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: -- about this question: "You mentioned the free territories, which territories do you mean?" And you said: "The free territory was all the territory that was under the control of the Army of Republika Srpska." And then you said: "... specifically in my case, we are talking about Doboj. They had a prison. There wasn't one in Derventa or Prnjavor. Doboj was the only place with a prison facility." Are you therefore describing Doboj town, as opposed to the whole of the municipality, as part of the free territories?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO LISICA
utterances.text: Is that the question?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, that's the question, yes.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO LISICA
utterances.text: Well, as I told I, the military judiciary was inoperable. And this was -- unavoidable solution. Because wherever there were military courts, the prisoners were brought before a military judge, usually at the rear command posts. They would be interrogated there, members of the enemy forces, and then the judge would decide the next course of action. Since we had only a security officer either at the rear command post or at my command post, it was he who interrogated those who were of interest and then proceeded them to civilian authorities. But civilian authorities were not competent and they didn't have adequate skill to try the prisoners. But I didn't know what to do with them.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... just answer the --

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO LISICA
utterances.text: They were a burden. I had to send them away. And there was a prison in Doboj as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: General, truthfully you must just answer the question I ask, because I really don't have very much time today. All I was asking you: Whether you considered Doboj town to be part of what you call the free territory.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO LISICA
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. And one last thing - and I think then it will be time for the break - on this question of co-operation and prisoners. You were asked whether --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And this is at the next page in English.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And it's page 33 in your language. "Would civilians also be interviewed when they -- when you know they are civilians?" And you said: [As read] "Of course. But you have to understand: civilians are not captured. Where would I find a civilian in the middle of combat? There is not a possibility that I would capture a civilian. If you are talking about combat operations, there is no civilians in combat operations ..." Do you remember saying that?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO LISICA
utterances.text: Yes, I do. And that is correct. However, this propaganda about us committing rapes, there was no one to be raped. There were only military and police on the ground. But the western propaganda persisted and insisted on us raping and strangling people, et cetera. Please go ahead. I'm happy with my answer.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, you mentioned this in your interview, the question of rape. What you're describing, therefore, finally on this topic, as combat operations is two opposing forces fighting each other; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO LISICA
utterances.text: That's right. Two armed crowds, I would call them. Unprofessional nations or armed people. Two armed peoples. The Serbian army was not a professional one except in name only, and that applied to the Muslims and Croats equally. And this kind of unprofessional army was not subject to any regulations. It was a matter of survival. However, you prosecuted only the crimes committed by us, and you didn't try any Croats or Muslims, and this only exacerbates the hatred between these three peoples.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sir, you've made your feelings clear, and it's been pointed out to you before that you're mistaken in this. But we'll take it as read: You regard this Tribunal as biased.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, that's probably an appropriate moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: So we reconvene in 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: General, I've been asked to confirm, and I do so: When you describe "free territory," you meant territory that was actually controlled by the VRS; that's right, isn't it? Can you just answer "yes" or "no"?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO LISICA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I want to move, please, to Mr. Ninkovic that the Trial Chamber asked you about before. You and he, to put it at its lowest, did not get on very well, did you?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO LISICA
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And let's just have a look, please, at the exchange, part of the exchange of letters that you had.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Could we have a look, please, at document which is 30028. It's tab 7A.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And it's actually extracted from one of the books you wrote, General. While we're waiting for it to come up - I think it's all right - you wrote two books about 1992 or your experiences during the war.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO LISICA
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, this is -- comes from your book and is your, if you like, summary of the letter which is to come. You recognise that; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO LISICA
utterances.text: Yes, I recognise it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And let's go, please, to the next page in B/C/S and English.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And you put in a photocopy of your letter.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO LISICA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And it's dated the 4th of July. And it's to the Doboj Crisis Staff. And let's summarise it because it's quite a long letter. You talked about accusations that he was making.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And if we go to the next page in both English and B/C/S, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Paragraph 4: [As read] "If the gentlemen think that I and my army will take over territories for them, while you, People's Deputy, Doboj Crisis Staff member, and those in Derventa, Brod, and Prnjavor, will become what you think you are and that you are irreplaceable. Where are you taking the Serbian people. The people will not allow it - my deputy." And then you talk about a legal state, not a political one. And People's Deputy should know that there's no such thing as honest authorities, and so on and so forth. In summary, you were complaining, weren't you, that Mr. Ninkovic and the SDS were taking credit for, as it were, the creation of the Serbian state, which you believed was due to the army?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO LISICA
utterances.text: Well, roughly speaking, that's correct. I may go into details and try to explain to you, but I see that you understand. Because basically you know there's always a distinction between politicians and soldier, everywhere, in the west and elsewhere. They try to win people with the demagogy, whereas one has to do practical things in real life. So this was more a theoretical conflict rather than a quarrel. There was nothing for us to quarrel about. He was subordinated to me at the time in my territory. I had mobilised him for a certain period of times, but then an intervention came from above that he, as a people's deputy, shouldn't be mobilised and that he had more important business to do, though I never understood what that business was.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can we then look, please, at his response to you, which is 20044, and it's at tab 8.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO LISICA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So one --

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO LISICA
utterances.text: I was against Crisis Staffs. What is a Crisis Staff? The whole country was in crisis. If you have a command and you have a municipality, why do you need a Crisis Staff? But these were theoretical disagreements.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: General, again, can we just stick to the question I'm going to ask you about this. He -- he writes back to you on the 8th of July. He talks in this first paragraph of there being four letters from you. In fact, you've only got one in your book, and I don't think we've got the others. And then in the second paragraph - do you see? - he says: "With it you probably wanted to again establish how the civilian government in Doboj is corrupted, how it is absolutely not working, so it would be best to replace it with a military administration." Was that your view, General, that, really, everything should have been run by the military? That the country would have been better off if that were right?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO LISICA
utterances.text: No, that was not my general position. There're bad leaders and good leaders everywhere. Just like you have good officers and bad officers, army officers. But during the war, I thought that this gentleman didn't address substantial issues, which is to have the town functioning at all levels properly. There was some government, but it can always be better, and my intention is to improve it. If you ask them how many civilians were in captivity, taken by the Muslims or Croats to the camps, they couldn't produce a list. They didn't have any such information. I hope you are satisfied with my answer. I am.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And then he complains that you had absolutely no right or reason to bring his name in connection with looting or other illegal action.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And then if we go, please, to the next page in English, and it's still the same page in -- if we move it up slightly so that the General can see. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: He says he wants to inform you of the following: "The Crisis Staff of the Serb municipality of Doboj did not come into existence during or after but before the start of the combat for the liberation of the territories of the Serb municipality ..." And then at number 3.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So we need the next page, please, in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: "The Crisis Staff of the Serb municipality of Doboj was not brought to power but, rather, with the help of the army and the police of the Serb people of the Doboj municipality, it helped to organise and liberate all the Serb territories in the municipality." Now, you were not in Doboj at the time of the liberation, if you like, but were you aware that there had been a combined political, military, and police action to take over the town?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO LISICA
utterances.text: I don't understand your question. Doboj was liberated back in 1945. That's when it was liberated.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. All right. Well, the next paragraph, it -- it deals with it: "Even though ... one-third of the residents of Doboj municipality were of Serb nationality ..." Were you aware that in May, beginning of May of 1992, there was a combined military, police, and political action to place the Serbs in power in Doboj town?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO LISICA
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that. But no action or operation was needed anyway. Because in a civil war, as I said, birds of a feather flock together. You can't speak about ethnic cleansing because people instinctively flee to the area where they are in majority. Nobody was ordering anyone. If you shell Sarajevo and you kill one Serb, then you can hang me here for that crime. But you cannot even do that, because there are no Serbs in Sarajevo any longer. 99.something per cent are Muslim and there are a few Croats. And the same situation prevails in Central Bosnia. So this is all propaganda, this notion of ethnic cleansing. What it means was people were fleeing from one group to another without anyone ordering them to do so.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... yes --

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO LISICA
utterances.text: Please. I gave you an answer.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, you didn't give me an answer. Because it was a simple question: Did you know that -- that power had -- right.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO LISICA
utterances.text: I didn't know about this.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And, in fact, to cut this short, because you probably -- you remember Mr. Ninkovic's letter, he complained that your allegations were not true, and he asked you at the end of letter, please --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: If we go to the last page in English, and it's the last page in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: He wants you to come and meet him so you can see the results of the work and wants you to withdraw the claims. First question: Did you go and see him after he sent you this letter?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO LISICA
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did you withdraw the claims you'd made in the letter of the 2nd of July? Which unfortunately we don't have.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO LISICA
utterances.text: No, I didn't. He came to see me and he apologised.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. So he came to see you and he apologised to you.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO LISICA
utterances.text: Yes, yes. They all apologised. That's how things were. I wasn't prepared to tolerate anything. Why would I apologise to anyone? It wasn't me who started the war. I never wanted it. I just happened to be at the head of an armed people, and I defended this people. So these were political and demagogical disputes. But at the time I was not in the mood to have this kind of debates with him.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Would it be fair to say that because of your personality and because you were head of the army in that area, Mr. Ninkovic and Mr. Bjelosevic were, to a certain extent, frightened of you?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO LISICA
utterances.text: Yes, they were.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, may these letters please be exhibited and marked.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, we do object. I don't see particular relevance of these documents at all for the -- for the issues in this case. And I believe the witness said: "So these were political and demagogical disputes," and I didn't have time for that at that moment. I don't know -- I don't understand why is Ms. Korner trying to offer this document. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, could I ask -- would Your Honours be kind enough to ask the General to take his earphones off for a moment?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes. Could you please remove your headphones.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, what our case is with General Lisica is very much to the extent that, as he's more or less said now, some of the letters one sees and some of the actions are, in fact, the result of the General's personality. And these letters reflect, we say, very much his personality. And, in addition, they are, of course, relevant to the -- the -- the general evidence in respect of the take-over of Doboj.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Isn't his answer to your question as you summarise this series dealing with the questions sufficient? Isn't that the point of -- to which you were leading up to which he -- he readily embraced your suggestion?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, yes. But nonetheless, they're still relevant. I mean that -- nobody's said they're not relevant. And they also deal with the issue of what happened in Doboj. Now, Your Honours, at the time that we were putting in evidence about Doboj, we didn't put these in because we had other documents, but they've now become relevant and, we say, admissible. And if you look at the contents, it's clearly relevant. [Microphone not activated] And, Your Honours, can I point out also that Your Honours put down this topic - thank you very much - as the relationship with Ninkovic as part of the reason why this witness was here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. But I do agree that Your Honours put that as an issue. And, again, as Your Honours correctly put it, the -- what we have on the transcript is -- the witness confirmed that. And I don't -- I still don't understand how this document is relevant at all. This is a letter which Ninkovic is sending to General over some quarrel that they have between them, and this cannot -- this cannot serve as any -- any exhibit that would -- that would help or assist the Trial Chamber in finding the issues that Ms. Korner was mentioning. Moreover, it was up to the Prosecutor to introduce this document in -- as a part of their case, or during the cross-examination of witnesses. Because we went through Doboj, we had Andrija Bjelosevic here, we had rebuttal witness, and now only after all that we are faced now with the additional documents that -- that the Prosecution is now seeking to tender. We do object.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, with respect, I couldn't have put this to any of the witnesses from Doboj because Mr. Ninkovic has never been a witness. Mr. Bjelosevic wasn't -- no one's to believe Mr. Bjelosevic was aware of this correspondence. You have here the witness. Your Honours, we're entitled to explore, within Your Honours' limited, as it were, overview of what the witness may deal with, issues which go directly to this case. And one of the issues is, indeed, not just Mr. -- General Lisica's relationship with Ninkovic, but also the -- what happened in Doboj. And this is a relevant and admissible document. It doesn't have to go to General Lisica's, if you like, credit, or outlook. It can also be evidence, and it's there, if you look at what's said by Mr. Ninkovic, which advances the evidence in the case about Doboj, which is one of the municipalities in the indictment. And the fact that we didn't put it in as part of our case is because we had a limitation. As I say, we had no witness we could put this to. And now we do.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry to stand up again. But, clearly, Your Honours, the -- this letter was written by a third person. General here says: I didn't accept that and I didn't apologise to him. He came to apologise to me. Now, quite the opposite from -- from that what we have on the record, Ms. Korner offers this -- this document for -- for the truth of its contents. I mean, the -- actually, the -- the testimony that we have on the record opposes this document's credibility or the contents of it as credible. I don't really see the basis for that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm sorry, it does not. He says he doesn't know about the take-over. This is a declaration against Mr. Ninkovic's interest, if you like, where he says the Crisis Staff came to an existence before the start of the combat. This is page -- the second page of the letter in English, if we can go back to it. And Your Honours specifically said to General Lisica he was being called to deal with matters that might highlight the evidence that they had heard in the case. Now, here is Mr. Ninkovic saying to General Lisica, who received this letter. He did say he didn't apologise. General says he doesn't know about this aspect of it. The Crisis Staff was not brought to power [indiscernible] but with the help of the army and the police, even though only a third of the residents of Doboj municipality. That's all relevant evidence in this case. And the fact that it comes in at this stage, we say, is neither here nor there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mrs. Korner, what -- which -- which documents are we talking about precisely? It's -- it's 7A and 8?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, if we were to admit the letter that's presently up, I think your application also embraces an excerpt from the book. Why should that be added?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] You mean the letter from the General to --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You mean the first one? They're both -- [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... tab 8. We're talking about tab 8, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, it's tab 8 I specifically want in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Yes?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: So the question is, suppose that we admit it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Oh, do I want 7A as well?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No. I can live without 7A. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: So the letter is admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P2456 [Realtime transcript read in error "P2466], Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: General, next, briefly: Mr. Bjelosevic; you've already described your relationship with him. What you said to us in interview about him was that you -- the two of you had a good relationship. That would be right, would it?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO LISICA
utterances.text: That's right. I was on good terms with everyone.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You said at page 95 - and I'm not going to ask for it to be brought up. "We would always find a mutually agreeable solution of what is best in the cause of the defence of territory and the people."

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO LISICA
utterances.text: That is right. We shared the same goal and task but as part of different hierarchies or structures. There was no reason not to agree on something. We were on the same side and not on the opposing sides. We had a common enemy. If there is a difference of opinion, then people engage in discussions that need not necessarily amount to arguments. Even this issue with Ninkovic is something I don't see as an argument or a conflict, because otherwise someone may have ended up in prison. We simply had different points of view. Since I was in a more senior position, I simply had the last say. I told him to keep quiet and that things would be the way I decided, be it for Ninkovic or Bjelosevic.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, quite. I think you've explained that. You said at page 85 that you had informal meetings with him and that sometimes this would be when he was touring, as it were, inspecting the police who were on the front lines; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO LISICA
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And as you said on -- said on a number of occasions, effectively, all of you, the political, the police, and the army, shared the same goals. And the ultimate goal was this, wasn't it: To establish and control the territories declared to be part of the Republika Srpska, as it became?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO LISICA
utterances.text: Correct. Correct. Well, we did think it would still be Yugoslavia, but in the end it was Republika Srpska and Bosnia-Herzegovina which had never been a state, a country of its own. But NATO became involved and they had the might and dictated the terms. There's no mention of any democracy there. It's just power.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Now let's turn to the general question that you were asked earlier today by the Judges about resubordination of the police. And look at what I said in interview -- what you said in interview was -- what you said in interview was correct. First, is at page 28. Well, in fact, it started --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry, can we have the interview up again, please. It's 30012, and it's page 27 -- well, no. Let's start at page 28. 28 in English; and 24 in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... yep. "Srpsko" is coming up.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO LISICA
utterances.text: As the language called "B/C/S" is non-existent. I only heard of it here. There is Serbian, though.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Don't sidetrack.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO LISICA
utterances.text: Well, you can't keep taking away things from me all the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... all right. In fact, the question started the previous page, and I'm not going to trouble you with that, because you were asked to tell us about resubordination by the police to the army. And then you said, as you told us today: "The general principle was all the resources available to a military commander in his area of responsibility are subordinated to the commander. That means the presidents of municipal assemblies, Derventa," blah, blah, blah, "including the police in such a territory, civilian police." And you were asked then: "Was it war-time or peacetime?" And you said: "Only in the cases of an existence of the state of war." And then at the bottom of that page you explained about the one single task is the defence of the territory and the defence of the people. Now, you then went on to explain, at page 30 in English and 26 in Serbian.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO LISICA
utterances.text: I agree with everything that's written there. I agree with myself. Everything that's on the paper is true. I said the truth.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Okay. Well, then you explain that if you have a large front line and you're lacking manpower, it's in the interest of the police and the interest of the people that the police are acting on behalf to defend the territory. And you said that the police commanders that you commanded over, they tried to explain to you the police were not a combat force, that the police were going to be used for the control of the territory, which in fact they were supposed to do, but you explained to them about the enemy took over the territory, there would be no territory to control. Now, I want to come to how the actual resubordination came about. Could we go, please, to what you said at page 32 in English and 27 in Serbian. You were asked: "Did you ever consider in your mind during this period that you had to make a request which had to be passed up the chain of command in order to use the police in combat operations?" And you said: [As read] "No. I just ordered in my area of operations. If we are talking about civilian police ... I think that the police requested approval up their [sic] chain of command. Let's take for an example, we have a police chief in Derventa. I put in a request. He forwards his request to his superior and then his superior forwards the request to, I don't know where, but let me tell you, in the end, they have to execute what I ordered. "Q. So you were aware that even if you gave the order, the police had to go up its own chain of command because you actually phrased this order as a request? "Yes, that's how I did it. It makes sense. It's a logical flow of sequence of events, but you have to consider that the chain of the command of the military and the chain up to Mladic and whoever and the chain of command of the police, they run in parallel to each other. Ultimately, they end up with the same goal, which is why we had to clashes, and everybody was aware ... probably there was lateral communication. They probably spoke to each other." So, just summarising what you were saying there, General: There are two chains of command - the police and the military. You had to phrase what you in your own mind considered to be an order as a request, didn't you, because that's what had to do be done in any time when no state of war had been declared?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO LISICA
utterances.text: In my area, we behaved if -- as if there was a state of war. In other words, I would call Milosevic [as interpreted] or another station -- police station commander and ordered him something, to do something. He could not oppose that. Such a procedure did not exist. But he was duty-bound probably to report to Bjelosevic and to the person who was in the seat of the minister of the interior in that non-existent state. And they probably would say, Do as you were told by the colonel. Otherwise, someone would have to go. Either myself or them. And that was impossible. I was indisputable in my own territory. It's not as if I'm saying one thing and was doing another. I did what I said. When I called a municipal president to report to my office, he was always there in five minutes. I don't even know how. When I asked Ninkovic or Bjelosevic to come to my office, they did. There was no choice. It wasn't as if they could say, I've got other things to do. When I said so, it was their only thing to do.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: General, I absolutely accept you terrified the life out of these people, and we'll see why in a minute. But the reality was - the way things properly should have been - that's what I'm putting to you - is that this had to be phrased as a request, and each request had to go up the chain of command, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO LISICA
utterances.text: That's probably true. I don't recall writing requests. I had no time. Maybe one of my desk officers did. When I said that I needed 100 policemen along a front line or a police patrol, then my assistant for security probably drew up this request, as you termed it, to forward it to Milosevic [as interpreted]. In any case, my order had to be seen through. For the most part. Such things were dealt with by my security assistant, because he also attended the meetings. It was all dealt with at the various meetings. If I needed the police, I requested that the commanders of brigades and independent battalions be in attendance as well as Bjelosevic or any other policeman.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Let's just move through as quickly as we can, because I want to show you some documents in a moment, what you said in interview. The top of the next page in English but the same page in B/C/S -- in Serbian language.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO LISICA
utterances.text: Serbian. Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... I changed it.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO LISICA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The question was: [As read] "When you used the police, when you ordered, as you say, the police to take part in combat operations, was there a time-limitation put upon it?" Your answer: [As read] "I took it upon myself to see that the use of police for combat means was as short as possible. It never depended upon me how long it would be. It depended on the complete situation at the front line. I was completely aware that the police had its own share of tasks to conduct according to the law that regulated their work and that the phenomenon where they'd found themselves under me was a temporary one."

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And then if we go down the page in English. It's the next page in B/C/S -- in Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: "Would the police be mixed amongst the army or would they be together in a unit? "As a unit. "Who would be their commander? "Their own police station commander. In total they would be subordinated, let's say, they were deployed within the area of responsibility of the brigade to the brigade commander." And that's right, is it?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO LISICA
utterances.text: Precisely. I agree with myself and what I said.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. And you -- you dealt with this a little later.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Please, at, again, 69, please, in English; 58 in Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You were dealing with the term "co-ordination" which appeared in one of the documents, and you said: [As read] "the civilian authorities had their own task. Co-ordination, is -- if you are going to use police, just means that the police are going to be attacking in a co-ordinated fashion with our military formations. If they are being put to combat use, not in a police task -- not in police use. This only refers to combat tasks. Then it's normal they should know I'm going attack towards this tree whilst you are going to attack towards that house." So the police were resubordinated to the military in your area for the purposes of combat, is that right, fighting? Fighting the other side.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO LISICA
utterances.text: Correct. Everyone had their own axis of attack or area of defence or a line of defence so as not to be exposed to friendly fire. One needed to know where the rest are and when the artillery or aviation were to come into play, as well as all other branches. It wasn't only the police or the army. There were tanks and assets, and it was my role as the commander to co-ordinate it all together so as to enable it to work smoothly as a Swiss watch.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, you were also asked --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can we go, please, to page 97 in English and 82 in Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: -- what would happen if this mutual agreement, particularly between you and Mr. Bjelosevic, didn't work?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO LISICA
utterances.text: It was impossible to happen. Well, what would have happened?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO LISICA
utterances.text: We can presume. What would happen if there were an earthquake here?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Accepting it didn't happen with Mr. Bjelosevic except over that exchange of letters. But this is -- I want you to look at, please, what you actually said about this. At page 97, you were asked: "For once your good relationship with Mr. Bjelosevic failed. And he said, My superiors in the ministry of the interior are supporting my position that the police should be withdrawn. What would have happened then?" And your answer, as you say again: "It never came to that. They knew me quite well and I knew them. And considering that we had mutual goals to achieve, I don't think it would ever have come to that." And so the question went on that: [As read] "Supposing Mr. Bjelosevic had said my superiors, the minister of the interior, has ordered my troops come back to ordinary duties, what would have happened then? "Then such an issue would need be resolved by the Main Staff and the Supreme Command. The minister -- the Ministry of the Interior, the Ministry of Defence, that is the chain of events that would be produced." And is that right?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO LISICA
utterances.text: That is correct. But when you discuss the good relationship between Bjelosevic and Lisica, I wasn't Lisica per se, and neither was he Bjelosevic as an individual. We were institutions and the common point was our good relationship. But we were the people representing different institutions. We were heads of commands, heads of units. And that is where things need to run smoothly. As for personal co-operation or personal position, that is unimportant in times of war. The situation demanded that the two institutions functioned well. You say, If that would have happened. First of all, it was impossible for it to happen. Even if it did, someone would have been made to go, either me or Bjelosevic. But that would be resolved by the Supreme Command and the Main Staff. But there could simply be no situation in which he would not execute my order.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. Well, I'm going to show you, as I say, in a moment, some documents which you may think support what you say about the chain of command. And I want to ask you one last thing about the interview. On disciplinary or criminal proceedings, you were asked the questions the Judges asked you this morning in -- or in interview last year.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can we look, please, at page 44 in English; 36 in Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You were asked: "If the civilian police unit is subordinated to the military, will this have an impact on the police disciplinary system?" And then the answers got slightly off track.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So can we go, please, to page 45 in English and 37 in Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I better read the whole part. [As read] "If during the course," you were asked, "of a period when you were using a police force for -- a police unit for combat operations a member of that police unit committed a crime or disciplinary offence, who would be responsible for dealing with it - the military or the police chain of command?" And your answer: "The police itself. But this is the way you should take it. Whilst being engaged in combat activity, a policeman does not have a lot of opportunity to commit a criminal act." You were given an example: A policeman took a civilian prisoner during combat operations and beat him up or killed him. Would you consider that a crime? You then say you gave an order. "If I find anybody who's killed a civilian, he better shoot himself or I will kill him." And then you -- the question: But supposing somebody was stupid enough to ignore your threat and do that? And you said he would be arrested and sent to prison. There is no mercy for such things. By whom would he be dealt with - the military or the police? And you said: The first one that manages to capture such a person. And then, it was asked -- a less dramatic scenario was put to you: "A policeman refuses to obey the order given to him by his unit commander," who you said would be the police commander, "who would deal with him - the military authority? "The police." Now, that's right, isn't it? That policemen, when resubordinated to the army, still remained policemen?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO LISICA
utterances.text: He was a policeman. But under a different hat.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO LISICA
utterances.text: Instead of patrolling the streets, he was in the trenches. But, nonetheless, a policeman. As I told you, our legal system had caved in. It was broken into pieces. In normal situations all this would have been handled by the military judiciary, starting with the level of battalion and up. Since that was non-existent, we had a military court in Banja Luka in the corps. There were many breaches of discipline that were under the jurisdiction of the military judiciary, but such things did not function, and I usually ended up in the position of a military judge. Well, not me personally, but my command.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: But the point is this, isn't it: There are certain crimes which could only be dealt with by the military courts in normal circumstances; that's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO LISICA
utterances.text: In war-time conditions, it is the military courts --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: But if a policeman committed a crime that was not a crime that came under the military court's jurisdiction whilst he was resubordinated to the army, he would be dealt with by the police chain of command themselves, would he not?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO LISICA
utterances.text: I don't understand the question. Why is it so important?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Never mind why it's important, General. You've got a unit of police, say, 200 of the Doboj special police that you acquired at some stage. And during the course of the time when they are resubordinated to your command or one of your officers, one of them commits a disciplinary offence. Would you, the army, take disciplinary action against him; or would it be left to the police?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO LISICA
utterances.text: The procedure: I would launch the procedure against a police officer who committed an offence during combat activity. Whatever is subordinated to me -- or, rather, not me, to the command of the brigade or the army, is dealt with by the army until it is taken out of its jurisdiction, until the man returns to his regular tasks. As a police member on the front line, he is subordinated to the commander, and the commander must deal with all his offences until the resubordination is in place. While he is subordinated to me, I deal with it; when he is subordinated to the police, the police does. That's logical. How else?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, but hang on a minute. Sorry. Have a look at your interview, what you said there. You were asked: "Who would deal with the man who, resubordinated, refuses to obey an order?" And you said there: "The police." Now --

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO LISICA
utterances.text: Military police.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You meant to say the military police; is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO LISICA
utterances.text: Military police, yes. That's what I meant. During combat activity, then the military police deals with it. When he is patrolling a village, then the civilian police deals with it; whereas, during combat activity, it's the military police. If you're talking about mistakes, but there couldn't be any mistakes. What kind of mistakes would those be?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: What powers did you as a military commander have to discipline a resubordinated police officer? Could you demote him?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO LISICA
utterances.text: He doesn't have a rank. How can I demote him? But these are theoretical questions. And that applies to peacetime. In war, it's very different. I don't care about his status, if he's a corporal, lieutenant, or whatever. For me, he is a fighter on the front line. While he's subordinated to him [as interpreted], he reports to me. When he is no longer there, then have them do to him whatever they want. But while he's under my authority, then I punish him for his offences, or I make proposals. But when I make a proposal, it must be done, that the police officer be demobilised or something like that. But then such things didn't happen. Then Milosevic [as interpreted] or whoever was the commander in charge, had to act upon that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... all right --

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO LISICA
utterances.text: There can be no opposing opinions here.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Okay. So what you're saying, as I understand it, is the police officer who, in your view, has committed an offence, you then tell Bjelosevic that he has got to demobilise him or do something to this officer; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO LISICA
utterances.text: Well, there is -- there are those who are in a position to draft such an order to implement what I ordered. But it had to be implemented. Whether it would be Bjelosevic or my assistant for security, that's a technical matter which I cannot comment. But when you say Commander Lisica, that actually means the command, and the command is an institution. And there are all elements there - security, intelligence, logistics, communications, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... yes. No, this is what --

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO LISICA
utterances.text: Somebody from my command would deal with it. And who would be the one to dictate the letter or type it out, I don't know. But the order would certainly be executed.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. So I think the point you're making, General, is this: You said earlier he didn't have a rank so couldn't demote him. He still, as you said, remained a police officer, but serving as part or serving as a resubordinated person to the military. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO LISICA
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And so if any action were to be taken against him, short of you're throwing him into prison or having him stood up at the wall and shot, it would have to be taken, it would have to be taken by the police, wouldn't it?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO LISICA
utterances.text: A court must pass a judgement to shoot somebody. It wasn't a private war. That would enable me to take a pistol and kill anybody. But since we didn't have courts, then it was up to the civilian courts to deal with that, because there is no execution without a court.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Well, can we just have a look, please, at --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Could we just have a look at a couple of -- well, more than a couple -- some of the documents on this issue of the police and resubordination. First of all, can we look at document which is 30016.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Tab?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Oh, tab 16.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: This is an order from the Krajina Corps dated the 5th of September -- sorry, to the command of the Krajina Corps from General Mladic, dated 5th of September. Saying: "Pursuant to the order issued by the Presidency of the Serbian Republic ..." And then it orders a battalion to be formed from the MUP in Prijedor. This is right, isn't it, General, whether you liked it or not, and I think you didn't much, that the Presidency or the president of the republic had the power to order both the Main Staff and the police, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO LISICA
utterances.text: Yes, he did. So what's unclear here? Of course they had that power. We called that the Supreme Command. I'm merely saying that in a non-existent state, from a legal point of view, there can be no Supreme Command either. But we had a Supreme Command anyway, in a non-existent state.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Then can we look, please, at document number --

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO LISICA
utterances.text: Other commanders also had areas of responsibility, but those areas were not investigated before this court, which is a sad fact for the people there.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can we look next, please, at -- actually, it's on the same point, the Presidency. Document, please, 30014. Tab 12.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: While that document is coming up, Ms. Korner, I alert you that when we rise at 1.45 your time would have been exhausted.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, I was hoping for five minutes more because of the time we went through on General Mladic's diary, which I think took about five minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: I'm assuming that that would have been taken account of.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Well, see how we go.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Could you look, please -- yes, we've got that document. Now, look, this is Zvornik, 25th of August, 1992. And it deals with the -- a company from the Zvornik public security station. And do you see that it says: [As read] "Based on the need to counter the offensive of the Green Berets, with the approval of the Ministry of the Interior of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina ..." So, do you agree, it appeared that, as you agreed, although not in your area, approval had to be given by the minister for the use of police troops?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Perhaps the witness can read the document, because I don't think that the translation is -- is proper. There is no approval here mentioned in the -- in the actual document.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Could you read the first -- under "order," could you read out, please, sir -- General. Could you read it out, please, aloud. Sorry, could you just read it out.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO LISICA
utterances.text: You want me to read it?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... yes, please, because we need a translation.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO LISICA
utterances.text: "Based on the needs expressed for the prevention of the offences of the Green Berets, and with the approval of the Ministry of the Interior of the Serbian Republic of BH, along the axis of Donja Kamenica village and Srpsko Snagovo I hereby order an intervention company of the Zvornik public security station is to be used as part of the Zvornik Brigade to close the axis Jasikovci village-Grujici village, with the task," et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... that's all right. Stop, stop, stop. Stop, stop, stop. That's enough. I didn't need you to read any further. Thank you. So, General, so do you see, as far as the Zvornik Brigade is concerned, the approval of the Ministry of Interior was obtained?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO LISICA
utterances.text: Well, that -- but here, too, approval was always given in Doboj. You make a phone call and they say, Okay, we approve. And then the correspondence follows.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, sorry, General, I understand that. And it may seem that I'm asking silly questions, but if you wouldn't mind just answering them. Can you have a look, please, at a further document, which is, please, at 30005. Tab 34. This is a report to the Drina Corps from Lieutenant-Colonel Andric. Did you know him?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO LISICA
utterances.text: I did not.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Who is saying, page 2 in English, paragraph 5: [As read] "Please resolve the issue of commanding (use) of the SJB unit (police) since they cite the decision of the Ministry of the Interior regarding their deployment (they are under their command and only the ministry can deploy them)." So it would appear that in areas outside ones that you controlled, General, the -- the system of getting approval from the minister, or the Ministry of the Interior, was followed; would you accept that?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Just if Ms. Korner can specify the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: December of 1992.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO LISICA
utterances.text: I think that it may seem that way on paper. Everything was done in agreement. The war and all the ministers of the police and the military commanders met daily. It was a living organism. They always talked. Of course, everybody tried to avoid being sent to combat. These people also complained when I wanted to do so. And they said, But our minister didn't give approval. And I would reply, I'm your minister now. The soldiers from other municipalities were requesting to be sent home and so on. Nobody likes war. They all wanted to be as far away from the front as possible. It was business as usual. I believe you English people understand that very well. You have war-time experience.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, I want to put as a series of sentences to you and see if you agree with them. Throughout the war the civilian police participated in battles through the area of the Republika Srpska. Do you agree?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO LISICA
utterances.text: I do, in principle.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: With the exception of a brief period in 1992, when it was resubordinated to army commands in its place of operation, it was mainly autonomous in action and under its own command.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO LISICA
utterances.text: I don't know of any police actions. Autonomous police actions, what kind of actions would that be? Maybe actions against some infiltrated sabotage group or criminals.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: If operations in the field were planned by the VRS Main Staff, it would send a request to the Supreme Commander for the engagement of police; and if the planning was being done by a corps, then its commander would address the MUP organ in the area in question for the engagement of their units. Do you agree with that statement.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO LISICA
utterances.text: Well, these are probably procedures that were followed. It always originates from the commander of the combat action. And then he involves people in the procedure, and these would be the commands of the military and the police. This was done to have everything covered legally, but that didn't halt the execution of the order.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Okay. You were involved in both the Bosanski Brod operation and the corridor operation. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO LISICA
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Do you agree with this statement: For both the Bosanski Brod operation and the corridor, in the case of planning, the Main Staff applied the Supreme Commander, Karadzic, who approved the use of MUP members? Were you aware of that? Or do you agree with that, rather?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO LISICA
utterances.text: I am not familiar with that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And now one final document, please. Could you have a look, please - the two final documents, I hope - at 30020. At tab 25. This is a report from Mr. Bjelosevic. He talks about the death of Mr. Bijelic. And then says the same day you turned up to the Derventa SJB, and this is October 1992, threw out the employees out of the SJB building, stopped the traffic, ordered the commander to report to you, and explained that the reason for these actions was to show the Derventa politician how they should work. And whilst hurling countless insults at them, you criticised their work. Is -- do you remember that incident? And is that a rough description of what happened?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO LISICA
utterances.text: No. I don't know. Well, it may be -- it may be correct. But I think I would remember if somebody had been killed. This says that somebody was killed, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Does it sound like something you might have done?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO LISICA
utterances.text: Bijelic. No. What did I stop? What does it say? "Three escorts, throw employees out of the SJB building ..."

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Don't worry about that. Can you look, please, finally at a document 00494. Tab 11. This is a report in July of 1992 from Colonel Vukelic. As you put it, the late Colonel Vukelic. And I want you to just look at something he said under paragraph 5, which is the next page in both English and B/C/S. Do you see he's saying: "Morale in the units is high, with the exception of Tactical Group 3, where erosion of morale has occurred because of the arrogant attitude of ..." you, Colonel Lisica, as you were then towards your subordinates, "... as well as his unprincipled treatment of some of the officers. He is arresting people one day and demanding their release the next day." I take it you wouldn't agree with that. But it's right, isn't it, that you did actually arrest -- or agree with the description of you as unprincipled, but you were ordering a number of people on a number of occasions to be arrested, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO LISICA
utterances.text: I agree with what Vukelic says. I was arrogant.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And then the last question that I have is this: You told the Court earlier on today that your powers and your opinion were derived from the ... the Strategy of Armed Combat; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO LISICA
utterances.text: I didn't understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry. You told the Court earlier today, when you were explaining to the Court, rather expansively, that in a time of war everything in your zone of responsibility came under your command. You said that came from the Strategy of Armed Combat. Is that right? Your powers.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO LISICA
utterances.text: That is right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Are you able to recall whereabouts, in what is a lengthy document, you say you derived those powers? Where it says that.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO LISICA
utterances.text: I derive it from a book that's called Strategy of Armed Combat. It was issued by the Supreme Command Staff of the SFRY and published by the SSNO. It was an official document, a public document.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... I absolutely -- no, I'm merely asking --

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO LISICA
utterances.text: But if you want an exact reference to article, paragraph, item, I'm unable to do that. We were taught at the Command Staff Academy in Belgrade and I had to read it, but where it is exactly to be found, on what page of the book, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. That's all I ask.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: So we take the luncheon break, and when we reconvene -- sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: I have one small issue with exhibit numbers. Madam Registrar, at page 39, line 16, we are at P2455. And at page 67, line 18, we jumped to 2466.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think that the number should be P2456. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: So we resume at 3.00, when cross-examination by the Defence would begin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: --- Luncheon recess taken at 1.49 p.m.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, just before the witness comes in for cross-examination by the Defence, I have an application; that is, to make the interview that was conducted with him an exhibit in this case. And the reason for that is this: At the beginning of his cross-examination by me, he said that he'd read it all, he agreed with it, and it was true. Although I managed to put certain parts to him in the limited time that I was allowed, I may say, I was not anticipating that his evidence to Your Honours would be quite so different. I have not managed to cover all the parts of the interview where he dealt with these topics. Just taking, as an example, at page 79 he was asked about the 200 men from Doboj, and he gave an answer at page 80. And there are a number of instances. So, in those circumstances, Your Honours, I would ask so that Your Honour can evaluate his evidence today to you with the answers he gave on those topics within the course of that whole interview. As I say, time limitations meant I couldn't possibly go through all the times he dealt with these topics.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: We object, Your Honours. First of all, in the course of the cross-examination it was put to the witness everything what he said in -- in his interview which -- which Ms. Korner was reading to him. So we have that all on the transcript. I don't see why is there a reason that we introduce another -- another document that is already in the -- on the record. Because she was reading from the interview and asking -- asking the witness to confirm that or not to confirm. And all the relevant parts, as far as I can see, are there. I don't think that -- that the -- that the application is justified. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Of course, what I understand her application to be is that notwithstanding the fact that she placed parts on the record, it's the parts that were not thus placed on the record that she wants in. Mr. Krgovic, do you have a view on this application?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, it was joint position.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, can I confirm that that's the point: That there are many parts which I simply didn't have time to put in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: The Chamber is of the view that we would not be assisted by having the entirety of this interview entered as an exhibit. And therefore the application is refused.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can I ask whether a -- as it were, a redacted one, in the sense of just dealing with the topics that Your Honours wanted to cover with this witness? Or is that just a blanket no? If you see what I mean. In other words, if we take out the -- obviously the interview contains a bit of to-ing and fro-ing, but if we -- if we just simply limit it and we obviously send it to the Defence in advance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Well, by its very nature, the -- an interview of a witness before he comes into court is -- serves the purpose of putting the calling party in the position -- well, principally the calling party in the position to know, having proofed the witness, to know where the witness is going. But there remains a distinction between that statement and the viva voce testimony which the practice and the Rules of the Chamber favour, so that between what the Chamber, whose witness he was, and the cross-examining parties, the relevant -- notwithstanding the witness's adoption of the contents of the interview in its entirety, the relevant parts have been put into the record. And we don't see why it's necessary to go further.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour, that's -- but that -- I don't mean to argue this one, but I just want to make this clear: My application was made because - simply because - there was such tight time limits put on the cross-examination. And as I say, I would have asked for more if I'd known what he was going to say to Your Honours. Not all the relevant parts have been put. That's -- that was my -- that's the reason for my application. Sorry, I don't want to argue Your Honours' ruling, but I just want to make it -- to ask whether you would consider just those parts not read into the record and which relate to the topics. That's all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, I think the point of the Chamber is that for the purposes of which this witness was called, it is the Chamber's opinion that you did, in fact, cover all the essential parts of his testimony dealing with resubordination. It is true, as you say, that you didn't cover all of them and that there are a few extra places or pieces of his testimony that actually also deal well it, but adding those to what we already have would make no difference.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I won't pursue the matter further. Then the only matter is this. Your Honours will recall that he referred and, indeed, my last question was in respect of the Strategy of Armed Combat which he referred to as the basis of what he asserted were his powers in a time of war. Your Honours, it is in fact an exhibit. Mr. Krgovic put it in. It's 2D160. But upon checking, we discovered although the whole manual is in, in B/C/S, only about three pages were apparently translated by the Defence. We didn't appreciate that until we checked. We've actually got a full translation. And what we propose to do, subject to Your Honours' and the Defence' agreement, as it is an exhibit, is to ask the Defence -- to supply the Defence with the full translation of the manual and ask for the translation to be uploaded into e-court together with the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: I do understand the technical position to be that in fact the exhibit is -- it's already an exhibit, but through oversight, or whatever, the English version is not physically with the Court and it's merely a matter of correcting that deficiency?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
