utterances.text: Your Honour, that's absolutely right. It's happened from time to time. But because it's a Defence exhibit, we can't upload the translation, so we have to provide it to the Defence to upload. But I just thought I'd -- I'd let Your Honours know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes. Well, by whatever it is necessary for us to order to facilitate this, we so order.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: So while the witness is on his way in, I would give the usual reminder to Defence counsel that the two hours that you have between you, it is up to you as to how you divide that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: I don't know who is going to begin. Mr. Cvijetic? Yes, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll have to cross-examine this witness because the last time the division of time was at my expense, so I'm going to do it this time. Good afternoon. And before I address you, I'm going to remind you of the question posed by the Presiding Judge as to how would you like to be addressed.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO LISICA
utterances.text: Slavko Lisica.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: How about General Lisica?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO LISICA
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, General Lisica, before I put the questions that I planned to ask you, I'm going to return a document shown to you by the Prosecution because I would like you to look at it again.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For the record, this is Exhibit P01764; page 228.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: While the usher is doing that, I would point out to the witness that when the witness and counsel both speak the same language, it is necessary for there to be a pause to allow the interpreters to catch up so there's no overlap. So after counsel would have completed his question, General, before you attempt to answer, just allow a few seconds for the interpretation. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: General, you remember this?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO LISICA
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I see that the Trial Chamber does not have the document on their screens yet, so I'd like to call up P01764.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Tab number, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's tab 35 from the OTP's binder.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now we have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: General, since you wrote books, I am seeking a linguistic interpretation from you. If you look at the bottom of the page, where it says "Talic," and then after "Talic," we have a colon; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO LISICA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: In our language, could this mean that these were Talic's words and then his words are being quoted? Now I'm just talking about a linguistic interpretation.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO LISICA
utterances.text: Yes. That is how it should be. It should be the words of Talic, and not Mladic, as it's written here.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Now, if you look at the original copy, can you see that there were some markings added in colour red?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO LISICA
utterances.text: Yes, yes, there are some additions.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: So, General, bearing in mind what you said about Mr. Mico Stanisic, you firmly can confirm that you never said that?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO LISICA
utterances.text: I couldn't have said that because I don't know the man.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Do you allow for the possibility, then, that somebody has reduced and abridged all the discussion so that, as the final product, it is impossible to determine who said what?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO LISICA
utterances.text: Yes, I do allow for that possibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, I'm going to move to the questions that I intended to ask you. And I would kindly ask the usher to give you a rather voluminous binder with documents which is intended for you. Now, please, the most practical course would be for you to extract document number 3, because I don't think you can handle the whole binder. If you look on the right-hand side, you will find the page number. And kindly take out document number 3. Take it out completely.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO LISICA
utterances.text: I was never good at office work.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Separate it from the binder because you'll have to read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry, I have to say for the record that this is exhibit from our library, 00051, from tab 3 of our Defence team. I think that we still have to wait for the document to appear on the screens. L00051. Or if it's easier: L51.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Now we have the document. And if it's no problem, can you please go straight to Article 173 of the Law on the Army, because this is that particular law; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO LISICA
utterances.text: Yes. This is the Law on the Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: So could you please go to Article 173.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And for the benefit of the Trial Chamber, we need page 24 in the English and page 17 in the Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Article 173. It's entitled: Command.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO LISICA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Have you found it?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO LISICA
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Now, General, this is a short article, so please read it first and then I'll ask you something. You don't have to read it out loud. Read it to yourself and then I'll put a question to you. Have you read it?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO LISICA
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: You will agree with me, won't you, that these are three basic principles of command in the army, although there are others, I know that there are others, but these three are fundamental ones; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO LISICA
utterances.text: Yes, you're right.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: The principle of unity of command with respect of the use of forces and resources means ... something that I hope that you are going to explain to us as briefly as possible, and I appreciate your assistance in doing so.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO LISICA
utterances.text: An officer, or a commander of a certain unit, as far as this principle is concerned, means that his orders must be obeyed.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry, we need to see Article 173 in English, so we have to move the right-hand part of the screen to the right, or scroll it up, because we need to see Article 173, and it's not there. Okay. But we have to move to another column because that's where it continues.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: So, in the army or in the combat zone or in the area of responsibility of a unit there is only one commander.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO LISICA
utterances.text: Yes. And he is the commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: There is no army in the world and there is no military commander anywhere in the world will allow to -- anyone to exert parallel command in his area.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO LISICA
utterances.text: If he were to allow that, he would be a bad commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: If in an area of responsibility of the unit commanded by this commander, let's say yourself, there are appeared an individual or a group that is participating in combat operations but refuses to listen to your command and are carrying out these operations according to their own principles of command, you are authorised either to put them under your command, to disarm them, and eventually arrest them if they committed some offences in the process.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO LISICA
utterances.text: You are absolutely right. I can only repeat what you said.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: There's no need for that. Let me move to the next principle. If you are in command, you can carry out your commands only if this third principle is in place. That is to say, that you can force all your subordinates to carry out your orders; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO LISICA
utterances.text: Precisely so.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: If you don't have that, then there is no command, there is no army, and the whole concept, the whole pyramid of military organisation will collapse; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO LISICA
utterances.text: Yes. Now let me explain to you --

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO LISICA
utterances.text: When I became commander of TG 3, which is an equivalent of a division, I was fortunate enough to have trained officers at my disposal because combat operations were being carried out along the corridor axis, and, therefore, I was able to appoint trained officers as brigade commanders, so I didn't have any problems with reporting. In other corps, however, they had many problems with the reserve forces but at the level of brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you about all this. Just a little patience, please. Now we are coming to which mechanism you can employ in order to force your subordinates to carry out your orders. If your subordinates refuse to carry out your order, in doing so they commit a criminal offence by refusing to obey the order of the commander in charge, and you are authorised through your security organ, or military police, or military prosecutor's office to hand over such principles to the judiciary for further prosecution. Now I'm just speaking about the principle. Don't tell me how it was in practice.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO LISICA
utterances.text: Yes. That is how it should be done.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: If your assessment is that a subordinate individual committed an offence which does not constitute a criminal offence, which means that he committed a minor offence or misdemeanour, you have the power, as well as the military disciplinary organ of the unit, to impose a disciplinary punishment upon him; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO LISICA
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: These disciplinary measures vary. One of those is the military remand prison or transfer. For those who hold ranks, suspension of further promotions, et cetera, et cetera. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO LISICA
utterances.text: Yes, it is. And they can also be dismissed from their post.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: The last measure that you mentioned, you can send someone from the rear to the forward front line so that can he experience how it is to be on the front line. Is that an option as well?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO LISICA
utterances.text: Yes, it is an option.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Now, General, we come to the next document that I would like to show you. Would you please take out document number 2 from the binder in front of you. And please don't put back the previous one, because we're going to deal with it a little bit after we have looked at number 2. So just open it and don't take it out.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO LISICA
utterances.text: I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Now go back to the first document, under tab 3, which we saw first, and I will provide the reference number for the other document once we get to it. But for the time being we'll remain with tab 3. Please go back to the first page of the Law on the Army, where the title of the law is.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So we are still with L51. We need the first page.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: General, please read for yourself Articles 2, 3, and 4.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO LISICA
utterances.text: Under number 2?

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Number 3, the Law on the Army.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO LISICA
utterances.text: Which articles?

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Two, 3, and 4. Have you read it?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO LISICA
utterances.text: I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: You will agree with me that we have a description of the complex military structure; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO LISICA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: In Article 4, we also have the hierarchy. In other words, who is responsible to whom. Basically, there's a general term for military personnel that is used, and we have the subcategories of the people who fall within that single category; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO LISICA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: That category includes reservists or military conscripts from the reserve while on duty. Is that something you can see in Article 3?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO LISICA
utterances.text: Yes, I can see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Go now to Article 9, please. There, we see that military units in certain cases are to be manned by people from the reserve force as well; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO LISICA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Now turn the next page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me see if the Judges have that on their screens as well. Yes, Article 9.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Which foresees that in the state of war or an imminent threat of war military units may be replenished with volunteers. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO LISICA
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: I can say that I have read all your books, documents, and interviews, and I recall your testimony. I know that you have a very poor opinion of volunteers as a category of people, especially those who took part in this war, but here we are merely discussing the legal concept of "volunteer." Such volunteers, by their being placed under military command, become military conscripts; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO LISICA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, could we -- could I ask Mr. Cvijetic to read out the definition from the law of what a volunteer is.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No problem. These are people who do not have their military assignment and were included in army ranks upon their own request.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Is that what it says?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO LISICA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... just read -- it doesn't talk about military rank.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: "War-time assignment" is what the translation is. "Volunteers are persons joining the army at their own request without a war-time assignment." Not a military assignment.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Did I say anything to the contrary? Subparagraph 3 of Article 9. I believe we are talking about the same thing.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, I'm sorry, but it may be important, as Your Honours know from discussions we've had. The English translation in the document is: "A volunteer has -- does not have a war-time assignment." The translation that came out over the earphones, when Mr. Cvijetic summarised it, was "military assignment." The two are not the same. The word is not the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know where the mistake lies, but the law does mention war-time assignment and I believe I read it out as such.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: It can be verified against audio recording.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: General Lisica, it is stipulated here that such persons are placed under military command, whereby they have the same rights and duties as military conscripts; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO LISICA
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, it includes both rights and duties.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Counsel, is there a difference between being a military conscript, on the one hand, and having the same - what was the word you used? - the same powers or the same functions as a military conscript? Duties. Sorry. What I'm hinting at is that being a military conscript is not necessarily the same as having similar duties.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have to confess that I do not understand your intervention. We can repeat the legal definition of these categories. The definition states that active military personnel and the reserve, while on military duty, enjoy the status of military personnel. That category includes military conscripts from the reserve force when executing their military duties. Is that clear now?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, what are you reading, please, Mr. Cvijetic? It's not clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Article 3, paragraph 2. So, reservists are considered military personnel while implementing their military duties. I believe that is sufficiently clear. We can use an example to try and clear it up for the general.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: General.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO LISICA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: People from the reserve force can do all sorts of things as civilians. They can be judges, attorneys-at-law, assembly deputies, ministers, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO LISICA
utterances.text: Yes. But such people usually do not make the reserve. At least not the categories you mention. But we had many waiters though. But in any case, in principle, it is possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Yes, I simply meant to say civilian professions. However, once there is a general mobilisation as an imminent threat of war had been declared first, all persons falling within the age band of 18 to 65, that is to say, all people from the reserve, including those who do not have a military assignment, are duty-bound to report to their respective military units; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO LISICA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: But, counsel, the -- to be -- to be labelled as belonging to the military reserve, would that not follow from the military assignment? So you, if we take you as an example: You're a counsel, you're a lawyer, an advocate, and in your military assignment it would say that you belong to the military reserve in case of a -- of a call-up; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, that is precisely the topic I wanted to discuss with the witness, but gradually. And we'll get to this particular issue. I was working my way up to a general call-up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Well, make sure that you elicit from the witness the position of people in whose military assignments there is no mention of belonging to the reserve.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will, Your Honour. That was the thrust of my questions. I was aiming to get there.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: So, General --

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO LISICA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: -- when all these people respond to a mobilisation, their civilian capacity ceases. And for you, as the commander, they are no longer attorneys-at-law, judges, or anything else. To you, they are military conscripts. In other words, soldiers. Correct?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO LISICA
utterances.text: In times of peace, units are formed where a military conscript is supposed to report to a particular command belonging to the unit where his military assignment is. In other words, every military conscript in peacetime knows what unit he belongs to, and is he to report to that unit or to that command where he had been informed to report to. That's in the briefest possible terms.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: So, all able-bodied men who reached the age of 18 were supposed to serve their military service.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO LISICA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Just wait. I have another question for you. Once they have served their military term, they are issued an important document called a military booklet; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO LISICA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: In the booklet, they have the beginning and end date of their military service.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO LISICA
utterances.text: Yes. As well as their military specialty.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Please do be patient. They also have the military evidentiary speciality, or VES; in other words, what they were trained during -- what they were trained in during their military service, their specialty.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO LISICA
utterances.text: Precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Any ranks are also mentioned, provided the person in question attended a school for reserve officers.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO LISICA
utterances.text: Yes. Or the rank of squad leader if they were exceptional soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: In other words, the rank of a commissioned or non-commissioned officer is mentioned if one such rank applies.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO LISICA
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Once the military service is over, such a person is under an obligation to report to a competent municipal organ when they are entered in the military register of the reserve force or reserve force military conscripts; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO LISICA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: His military booklet also mentions the war-time assignment you mentioned. In other words, the unit such a person is supposed to report to is mentioned in case of an imminent threat of war or state of war, including the assembly point where he is to report to; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO LISICA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Now I'm interested in the following. When one of them decides to attend training for a civilian policeman, they either attend an abbreviated policing course or enrol in a police school, whereupon they are -- become civilian policemen. Once they are civilian policemen, their status of a reserve military conscript is put on hold, and for as long as that person is performing police duties and tasks, such a person is not considered a military reserve conscript?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO LISICA
utterances.text: That is correct. And they probably attend military exercises --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: police exercises.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: However, when the status of imminent threat of war is declared, or the state of war, the situation changes, General Lisica. Then all from that age bracket, including civilian police officers and the minister of the interior, are duty-bound to respond to the call-up; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO LISICA
utterances.text: Correct. Yes, that's how it goes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: So that in the Ministry of the Interior from the minister down to the lowest-ranking employee everybody is a military conscript; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO LISICA
utterances.text: Yes. Under the law, that's how it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Throughout their tenure at the police, they still have a military booklet, don't they?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO LISICA
utterances.text: Yes, they do. If they served in the army. Although some police officers did not serve.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: General, if it is assessed that the situation is such as to require their participation in combat operations, they will have to get uniforms and weapons and will have to go to war; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO LISICA
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: If it is assessed that the situation does not require the participation of all of them in the war, they can discharge their regular duties, but the people's defence body in charge issues them a decision of labour or work obligation; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO LISICA
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: That work obligation is their war-time assignment. It is no longer their former civilian occupation, but becomes their war-time assignment given to them by the people's defence organ; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO LISICA
utterances.text: The work obligation usually coincides with the peacetime occupation so people can continue doing what they did before the war. My wife is an economist, and her work obligation involved continuing to work as an economist in the bank where she worked before.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: General, I'm reading to you the definition of work obligation. But we do agree that this is then their war-time assignment?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO LISICA
utterances.text: Yes, it is their war-time assignment.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: There's a reference to this in our legal library --

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO LISICA
utterances.text: And under that war-time assignment, they can be obliged to work longer hours. Instead of eight hours, say, ten hours or 15, whatever.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For the benefit of the Trial Chamber, this is L58 in our legal library, Article 2, and it's a decree on the organisation and discharge of work obligation for defence requirements.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: General Lisica, work obligation was no guarantee for any MUP staff that, as soon as the following day, they wouldn't be sent to combat wearing a uniform and carrying weapons; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO LISICA
utterances.text: In principle, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: However, the following situation is also possible: That, in a limited area, in the area of responsibility of one unit, the need arises to draft a certain number of police officers for a certain time. Can that happen?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO LISICA
utterances.text: Yes. Anything can happen in a war.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: General Lisica, the law provides for the possibility in such situations that the commanding officer in that area to carry out that mobilisation following the principle of resubordination. In other words, you can issue the order to resubordinate a number of police officers who will then have to join your soldiers in combat activities; right?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO LISICA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Once they join their -- join your unit to take part in combat operations, their civilian authority stops and they participate in combat operations with all rights and duties as everybody else; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO LISICA
utterances.text: Yes, that is precisely right.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Before we move on, go to document number 2 in your binder, please. L1 is the document. It's the Law on All People's Defence. Have you found it?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO LISICA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: I'm interested in Article 104. It's on page 67 in English; and in Serbian, on page 18.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO LISICA
utterances.text: I found it, 104.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Let's go to page 67 in English and on page 18 in Serbian. I suppose you've read it.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO LISICA
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: I won't repeat so as not to waste time. In other words, during the time they're resubordinated to you, they are military conscripts belonging to the category of reserve military conscripts. They are duty-bound to follow your orders and comply with the military laws and regulations.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO LISICA
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. That's exactly what the law says.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Do read Article 104. It is very important that we see that this applies both to the state of war and to the imminent threat of war; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO LISICA
utterances.text: Should I read it out?

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: No. Just confirm whether that's what the law says or not.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO LISICA
utterances.text: Yes. That's what the law says in Article 104.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: General Lisica, if they, as military conscripts, breach the principle that we have just discussed and commit some offence or disciplinary infraction while they have the status of military conscripts, they come under the jurisdiction of military, judiciary, and disciplinary bodies; right?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO LISICA
utterances.text: Yes. Exactly. Just like any other military conscript.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I've just been told that we should finish at 4.00. If that is correct, I can stop here; if not, I can continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excellent. Then I'll continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Let us now return to document number 7 in your binder. It is Exhibit P1284.07.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO LISICA
utterances.text: Item 7?

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: No. Just you go to Article 9. Let us just check if this is the right document. You already know which -- which law it is. It's the Law on Military Courts. Do go to the first page and I'll -- is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO LISICA
utterances.text: Law ... yes, yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Go to Article 9, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And for the benefit of the Trial Chamber, we are on page 2 of both linguistic versions.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Please read Article 9. Have you read it?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO LISICA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Article 9 outlines the jurisdiction of military courts who is tried by military courts for criminal offences, and Article 9 enumerates these persons.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO LISICA
utterances.text: Yes. They are enumerated here.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: But then you are mentioned here too. I hope you don't mind my saying that. It says an officer, because that follows from your status. These courts functioned both in peacetime and in war-time. Do you agree?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO LISICA
utterances.text: Yes, I agree. Nobody is above the law.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: A police officer, while he discharges the duties of a military conscript and while he is under your command, is tried by a military court for any criminal offence if committed during the discharge of his duties; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO LISICA
utterances.text: Yes, that is exactly how it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: So, from -- from ordinary theft to the worst war crime; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO LISICA
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, for the benefit of the transcript, I will now state the references that corroborate what has just been said. Exhibits 1D -- I may choose to show some to the witness, but I'll just give the references first.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, no, no, no. It is the "may corroborate." Mr. Cvijetic can show the documents to the witness and then we'll see where we get to.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. I will pick one. Just give me a minute.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for counsel, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's take tab 22; Exhibit 2D0017.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: General, you have found the document?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO LISICA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: It has only two pages. Have you found it?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, I dealt with this when I was asking the General questions. He said, in terms, he had no dealings with nor saw documents relating to the operation of the military courts, and therefore all he can do is comment on this. So I don't see where we're going to be taken.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He can comment.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry --

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You wanted me to show it. I just want to read out the references, but you wanted me to show a document. Why are you now backing out?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, no, Your Honours, I'm sorry. The General can deal with documents of which he has personal knowledge or understanding. He has, in terms, said he did not see any documents dealing with the running of the military prosecutor's office nor was he aware of the detail of the military courts. So he really cannot -- unless he says he's seen this document or knows about its contents, he cannot be asked about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Put another way, Mr. Cvijetic: Why would you be spending time dealing with a document such as this if you know from the answer that he has already given earlier that it -- he really can't speak to it?

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, that is not a problem. I don't want to embark on a polemic with Ms. Korner. But she insisted that I show a document from which it follows that military prosecutor's offices prosecuted all persons mentioned in Article 9 for any criminal offences from theft to war crime, and that is corroborated not only by this document but by all documents I wanted to list. But I will content myself with the witness's answer and continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: General Lisica, while they are subordinated to --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: Resubordinated to your command --

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: -- police officers, as military conscripts, as you said, are a legitimate military target for the opponent; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO LISICA
utterances.text: Yes. The same way that I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: All right. They also have certain rights and duties, just like you and other military conscripts. I will just mention some, and you say if you agree or disagree. Military laws and regulations are applied to their participation as well as international conventions dealing with military conscripts and soldiers; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO LISICA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Should they be wounded, they accord the status of military war-time invalid; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO LISICA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: If they get killed, their family gets the status of the family of a killed military conscript, or soldier; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO LISICA
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: While they are resubordinated, they must follow military rules and regulations, execute the orders of the military commander, and they have all other rights and duties that stem from their status as military conscripts; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO LISICA
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: And you have already answered this question. If they fail to abide by military laws and regulations, they can be held responsible; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO LISICA
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: I'm going to mention another right, and I would like you to confirm it for me. While they are conscripts under your command and they have a reserve-force rank, if they show valour during combat, the responsible command can promote them to a higher rank; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO LISICA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: And, lastly, a practical issue. If you, as a commander, think that they committed a disciplinary infraction, you can impose a disciplinary measure of a military remand prison, transfer, dismissal, and so on and so forth, to any police officer resubordinated to you; is that possible?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO LISICA
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: General, I'm now going to move to some practical matters relating to resubordination. I'm not going to show you any regulations. I'm just going to check first whether you are familiar with that in principle. In order to use the police force for military purposes and during combat, is something to be generally decided by the Commander-in-Chief of the armed forces? Are you familiar with that provision?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO LISICA
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: The Commander-in-Chief, who, as we all know, is normally a civilian, not a military person, has the right to issue orders, including an order to engage the police, and he can delegate this right to the commander of the Main Staff or the commander of a corps, a brigade commander, and I think that this right to use the police ends at the brigade level; am I right?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO LISICA
utterances.text: Yes, you are.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: I'm going to show you a document. It's tab 6 in your binder -- sorry, 62. 62. It's 1D00406. It seems you haven't found it yet.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO LISICA
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Just browse through it. I'm going to give you two or three minutes for that. And then we are going to discuss it. Will you quickly move to the next page, because we only have here the disposition of areas of responsibility.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO LISICA
utterances.text: Yes, it's all right.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: So, General Talic is making use of the legally provided authorisation on resubordination, and in this order where he designates the areas of responsibility of various units, and then towards the end of this order he states this in very specific terms, that in the course of carrying out combat operations all police forces shall be placed under the command of the zone commander and he is the one who decides on their use.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO LISICA
utterances.text: Yes, yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: So, General Lisica, for each and every --

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry. It seems that we have to move to the next page in English. Yes, that's it. Towards the bottom of the page.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: So, General, for each and every instance of resubordination that you carried out in the area of your unit, you had the basis in this order. And to all intents and purposes, you could have implemented this order simply by ordering the chief of the police station or the chief of the CSB to give a required number of policemen to you; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO LISICA
utterances.text: Yes. But we dealt with this in -- during the course of oral reporting.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Just be patient. We're coming to that. So, you personally could have issued such an order even in the absence of the order issued by General Talic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO LISICA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: If your assessment was that the situation on the ground is such that the territory within your area of responsibility could come under the enemy control, then you are entitled to recruit and draft the entire staff of a police station or even the entire personnel of a Security Services Centre; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO LISICA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Andrija Bjelosevic, while you were in communication with him, was in resubordination by virtue of this order; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO LISICA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: In response to a Prosecutor question, you gave us an extensive reply about the co-operation that you had with the police force. You would not issue any further orders to a police chief if he had previously already placed all his --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the speakers please pause between questions and answers. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: So you cannot issue an order to an SJB chief if he already has no police at his -- force at his disposal.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO LISICA
utterances.text: Of course I cannot. But it never happened that they were left completely without their staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: I'm talking about this issue in principle.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO LISICA
utterances.text: In principle, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: So, if you assess that the situation requires that, you can even engage only one police officer, if he hasn't got more.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO LISICA
utterances.text: In theory, but not in practice.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Now my next question concerns your communication with Andrija Bjelosevic and other SJB chiefs. Whatever the communication is, you have the last say. You -- you cut through the cord's knot and it's up to you to decide eventually.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO LISICA
utterances.text: Yes. That is the situation provided both in the law and in practice.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: So being a military commander, all your decisions have to be translated into orders; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO LISICA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: And pursuant to such orders, all those to whom these orders pertain must obey them regardless of any other agenda that they might have.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO LISICA
utterances.text: They must obey.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: There's an old military saying, which says: Carry out an order and then complain.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO LISICA
utterances.text: I used to repeat that during the war. If anybody didn't like any of my orders, I have to tell them, Carry it out first and then complain about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Sorry. This was exactly my question, because that applies to life in general. It is possible that a police chief has serious problems if he is left with a large -- without a large number of his police force, but he nevertheless has to carry out your order, and then, subsequently, he might put forward some comments to the command in charge for it to take into consideration the reality; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO LISICA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: General Lisica, I'm going to finish with two documents shown to you by Ms. Korner. They are from the Prosecutor's tab 12 and 35. Let me just remind you that this has to do with those cases in Zvornik. 3014 and 3005.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I suppose that this is an exhibit number. Because there's no indication that this is the case, maybe Ms. Korner can be of assistance.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] 65 ter.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. That's 65 ter 3005 and 3014; tabs 12 and 34.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Let me just briefly remind you, General: In the transcript, first, we have the wrong number then we have the correct numbers of tabs, which should be 12 and 34. Now, these examples that relate to Zvornik where there were some problems with resubordination was something that was caused, according to your words, by people refusing to go to the front line, et cetera. However, being lawyers, we have to deal with principles here. Now, this dispute that was described here could have resolved only in one way, and that is by the commander in charge issuing an appropriate order; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO LISICA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: General Lisica, I have concluded my cross-examination, and my learned friend, Mr. Aleksic, is probably going to continue tomorrow. Thank you for answering my questions.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO LISICA
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... it's almost time for break, so should I start now or tomorrow?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I just wanted -- Your Honours, I forgot, and indeed at the time I didn't think it was relevant, but the Defence having addressed it, I would like these two documents exhibited. It goes clearly now to the issue, that is, the one that Mr. Cvijetic has just referred to, which is given the number 30014, and the second document.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: If I correctly remember, over the last document we were talking, and Ms. Korner was complaining that the witness had nothing to do with that document, he was not aware of it, and there is no basis to introduce that document through this witness. And how is this a different situation at all? Because the witness doesn't know, doesn't know the facts behind it. We were talking about the principle, and I think the principle has been established. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, first of all, the witness can talk to this of his own knowledge because this is to do directly with the issue that he's been dealing with, namely command and control issues and the use of the police. It's completely different from military court documents about which, on his own a mission, he knows absolutely nothing. And the fact is, he does know something about this because he started to explain it. Mr. Cvijetic has gone back to it. And so I do think it's appropriate on an issue which has become such a hotly debated one, if I can put it that way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mercifully, we're at the point where we would take the adjournment for today, so we have a chance to remind ourselves as to what these documents are. General Lisica, we are about to take the adjournment for today. Your testimony would resume tomorrow morning when counsel for Zupljanin will begin their cross-examination. Overnight, I remind you that, having been sworn as a witness, that you cannot discuss your testimony with counsel from either side, or, indeed, inasmuch as are you a Chamber witness, with any of the legal officers of the Chamber. And in such communications as you would have with anybody else, you cannot discuss the testimony that are you giving before the Tribunal. So, with that, we would rise, and we would resume in this court -- courtroom tomorrow morning at 9.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Friday, the 2nd day of March, 2012, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 4.28 p.m.,
